questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Case: Kavya, a partner, is appointed to carry out the dissolution work. She is allowed a remuneration of Rs. 10,000. She has also agreed to bear the dissolution expenses up to Rs. 5,000. The actual dissolution expenses were Rs. 7,200, and Kavya paid all of them herself. What is the total amount debited to the Realisation Account for the remuneration and the expenses?
questions.explanation:
Remuneration: Realisation A/c Dr. To Kavya's Capital A/c, Rs. 10,000.
Expenses up to Rs. 5,000: Kavya bears these and paid them herself, so no entry is passed.
The excess of 7,200 − 5,000 = Rs. 2,200 is the firm's expense. Kavya paid it on the firm's behalf, so the entry is Realisation A/c Dr. To Kavya's Capital A/c, Rs. 2,200.
Total debited to Realisation A/c = 10,000 + 2,200 = Rs. 12,200.
Rs. 17,200 wrongly treats the entire expense as the firm's.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On dissolution of a firm, a loan advanced by a partner to the firm is repaid before the partners' capitals are repaid.
Reason (R): Under Section 48 of the Partnership Act, 1932, assets are applied first to pay third-party debts, then advances made by partners as distinguished from capital, and then the partners' capital.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. A partner's loan ranks ahead of capital in the order of settlement.
R is true. It correctly states the order laid down in Section 48. After capitals are repaid, any residue is divided in the profit sharing ratio.
R directly explains why the partner's loan is paid before capital.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: According to Section 48 of the Partnership Act, 1932, losses (including deficiencies of capital) on dissolution are to be met in which order?
options: Capital of partners → profits → partners individually in capital ratio
Partners individually in profit-sharing ratio → profits → capital
Profits → capital of partners → partners individually in profit-sharing ratio
Profits → partners individually in equal ratio → capital of partners
questions.explanation:
Section 48(a) says losses, including deficiencies of capital, are paid first out of profits.
Next, they are paid out of the partners' capital.
Lastly, if still needed, the partners pay individually in their profit-sharing ratio.
Option (1) wrongly puts capital first and uses the capital ratio, which applies only under Garner vs Murray to an insolvent partner's deficiency.
Answer: (3)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following events result in dissolution of partnership, as per NCERT?
(i) Change in the existing profit-sharing ratio
(ii) Admission of a new partner
(iii) Death of a partner
(iv) A partner introducing additional capital with no change in the profit-sharing ratio or in the partners
(v) Expiry of the period, where the partnership was for a fixed term
(vi) The firm taking a loan from a bank
questions.explanation:
(i) Yes: a change in profit-sharing ratio is listed.
(ii) Yes: admission is listed.
(iii) Yes: death is listed.
(iv) No: the partners and their ratio stay the same, so the existing relationship does not change.
(v) Yes: expiry of the term is listed.
(vi) No: a bank loan is an ordinary business transaction.
So 4 events result in dissolution of partnership.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the following statements:
Statement I: Dissolution of a partnership firm necessarily brings about dissolution of the partnership.
Statement II: Dissolution of a partnership, for example on the admission of a new partner, necessarily brings about dissolution of the firm.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.explanation:
Statement I is true. When the firm is dissolved, the relationship between all the partners ends, so the partnership also ends.
Statement II is false. On admission, retirement or death of a partner, only the existing partnership is dissolved. The firm may continue its business under the same name.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, an old computer that had been fully written off in an earlier year is taken over by Nitin, a partner, for Rs. 3,000. Which journal entry records this?
options: Bank A/c Dr. 3,000 To Realisation A/c 3,000
Nitin's Capital A/c Dr. 3,000 To Realisation A/c 3,000
Realisation A/c Dr. 3,000 To Nitin's Capital A/c 3,000
Nitin's Capital A/c Dr. 3,000 To Computer A/c 3,000
questions.explanation:
The computer is an unrecorded asset because it no longer appears in the books. When a partner takes over an asset, his capital account is debited and Realisation Account is credited, since the firm realises value from the asset.
Option (1) would apply only if the computer were sold for cash.
Option (3) is the entry for a liability that a partner takes over.
Option (4) is wrong because no Computer Account exists after the asset was written off.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: According to Section 39 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the 'dissolution of a firm' means:
options: Dissolution of partnership between all the partners of a firm
Breaking of relationship between any one partner and the remaining partners
A change in the existing profit-sharing ratio among the partners
Admission of a new partner into an existing firm
questions.explanation:
Section 39 defines dissolution of a firm as the dissolution of partnership between all the partners of the firm.
The Act separates two situations. When the relationship ends among all partners, the firm is dissolved. When it changes only for some partners, as in retirement, admission or a change in ratio, only the partnership is dissolved.
Option (2) is the tempting choice. A break with only one partner is reconstitution, and the firm can continue.
Options (3) and (4) also describe reconstitution, not dissolution of the firm.
Answer: (1)

questions.question:
Match List-I (transaction on dissolution) with List-II (treatment):
List-I
A. Creditor accepts furniture in full settlement of his dues
B. Creditor accepts a building worth more than his dues and pays the difference to the firm
C. A partner agrees to pay the firm's bills payable
D. An unrecorded liability is paid by the firm
List-II
(i) Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
(ii) Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iii) No entry
(iv) Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
options: A-(iii), B-(ii), C-(iv), D-(i)
A-(iv), B-(i), C-(iii), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(i), C-(ii), D-(iv)
A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii)
questions.explanation:
A-(iii): An asset accepted in full settlement needs no entry. Both the asset and the creditor already sit in the Realisation Account.
B-(i): The creditor pays the difference, so cash comes in: Bank Dr. To Realisation.
C-(iv): The partner pays on the firm's behalf, so his Capital Account is credited.
D-(ii): The firm pays an unrecorded liability in cash: Realisation Dr. To Bank.
Answer: (4)

Read the following statements:
Statement I: Dissolution of a partnership firm necessarily involves dissolution of the partnership.
Statement II: Dissolution of a partnership necessarily involves dissolution of the firm.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct. When a firm is dissolved, the relationship between all the partners ends, so the partnership also ends.
Statement II is incorrect. On admission, retirement or death of a partner, the old partnership is dissolved, but the firm may continue its business.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following events results in the compulsory dissolution of a partnership firm?
options: A partner becomes of unsound mind
The business of the firm becomes illegal
The fixed term for which the firm was constituted expires
A partner dies
questions.explanation:
Compulsory dissolution occurs when:
(i) all partners, or all but one, become insolvent;
(ii) the business becomes illegal; or
(iii) an event makes it unlawful to carry on the business.
Insanity of a partner is a ground for dissolution by court, which requires a partner's suit.
Expiry of a fixed term and death of a partner are contingencies. They dissolve the firm only subject to the contract between the partners.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Under Section 48 of the Partnership Act 1932, the assets of a dissolved firm (in the absence of an agreement) are applied for:
(i) paying partners' loans and advances
(ii) paying partners' capital balances
(iii) paying debts of the firm to third parties
(iv) dividing the residue among partners
Which is the correct order of application?
options: (i), (iii), (ii), (iv)
(iii), (ii), (i), (iv)
(iii), (i), (ii), (iv)
(ii), (i), (iii), (iv)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Debts to third parties are paid first. Secured loans take precedence over unsecured ones.
Step 2: Partners' loans and advances, as distinguished from capital, are paid next.
Step 3: Partners' capital balances are paid after that.
Step 4: Any residue is divided among partners in their profit sharing ratio.
Option (2) is wrong because it pays capital before partners' loans.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: According to Section 39 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the dissolution of a firm means:
options: Dissolution of partnership between some of the partners of the firm
Dissolution of partnership between all the partners of the firm
Retirement of a partner with the consent of the others
Change in the existing profit-sharing ratio of the partners
questions.explanation:
Section 39 calls the dissolution of partnership between all the partners of a firm the dissolution of the firm.
The Act separates the breaking of the relationship among all partners from its breaking among only some partners.
Options (1), (3) and (4) describe a break among some partners only. That is dissolution of partnership, or reconstitution, and the firm may continue.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (balance at dissolution) with List-II (treatment):
List-I
A. Investment Fluctuation Fund
B. General Reserve
C. Partner's Current Account (credit balance)
D. Partner's Loan (liabilities side)
List-II
1. Credited to Realisation Account
2. Distributed to partners' capital accounts in profit sharing ratio
3. Closed by transfer to that partner's capital account
4. Paid directly through Bank, not routed through Realisation Account
questions.explanation:
A-1: The format in Fig 4.1 shows the Investment Fluctuation Fund on the credit side of the Realisation Account.
B-2: Accumulated profits such as general reserve are credited to partners' capital accounts in their profit sharing ratio.
C-3: Partners' current accounts are transferred to their respective capital accounts.
D-4: A partner's loan is not transferred to the Realisation Account. It is repaid through Bank (Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c).
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: After a partnership firm is dissolved, which of the following activities can still be carried on in the name of the firm?
options: Accepting fresh orders from regular customers
Purchasing new stock to keep the business running
Admitting a new partner to bring in capital
Selling the firm's assets and paying off its liabilities
questions.explanation:
Dissolution of a firm ends its existence. No business is transacted after dissolution except activities connected with closing the firm.
Winding up means selling the firm's assets, paying its liabilities and settling the claims of the partners.
Fresh orders, new stock purchases and admission of a partner are acts of continuing the business, so they are not allowed.
Answer: (4)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
A firm of A and B (sharing profits 3 : 2) is dissolved. After all assets are realised and realisation expenses are paid, ₹1,25,000 is available in cash. The firm owes:
• Secured bank loan ₹60,000
• Unsecured creditors ₹40,000
• Loan from partner A ₹30,000
• Loan from partner B ₹20,000
Applying Section 48, what amount will A receive towards his loan?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Outside debts are paid first, secured before unsecured: 60,000 + 40,000 = ₹1,00,000. Balance left = 1,25,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹25,000.
Step 2: Partners' loans total ₹50,000 but only ₹25,000 is available. They are paid proportionately to the loans, in the ratio 30,000 : 20,000 = 3 : 2.
Step 3: A gets 25,000 × 3/5 = ₹15,000 and B gets ₹10,000. Nothing is left for capital.
Option (2), ₹12,500, wrongly splits equally. Note that the proportion follows the loan amounts, not the profit sharing ratio, even though both happen to be 3 : 2 here.
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (situation on dissolution) with List-II (entry):
List-I
(A) Expenses paid by the firm; no partner bears them
(B) Expenses paid by a partner on behalf of the firm
(C) Partner agreed to bear expenses; firm paid them
(D) Partner agreed to bear expenses and paid them himself
List-II
(i) No entry
(ii) Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iii) Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iv) Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
options: A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(i)
A-(iii), B-(ii), C-(iv), D-(i)
A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)
questions.explanation:
(A) The firm's own expense, paid in cash: Realisation Dr., Bank Cr. → (iii).
(B) The firm's expense, but the partner paid it, so the firm owes him: Realisation Dr., Capital Cr. → (iv).
(C) The partner's burden, but the firm paid: Capital Dr., Bank Cr. → (ii).
(D) The partner's burden and the partner paid: no entry → (i).
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following statements about closing the books on dissolution are correct?
(i) A loan given to the firm by a partner is not transferred to the Realisation Account.
(ii) A loan given to the firm by a partner's husband or wife is transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account.
(iii) If the cash left after paying outside creditors cannot fully repay partners' loans, those loans are repaid in the profit sharing ratio.
(iv) The total finally paid to partners on capital account equals the cash/bank balance left after all other payments.
(v) A partner whose capital account shows a debit balance after all adjustments is paid that amount by the firm.
questions.explanation:
(i) Correct: a partner's loan is paid directly through the bank, after outside creditors.
(ii) Correct: a spouse is an outside party, so the loan is an external liability (e.g., Mrs. Ashwani's loan).
(iii) Incorrect: partners' loans are repaid proportionately to the amounts due, not in the profit sharing ratio.
(iv) Correct: the aggregate payable to partners must equal the cash and bank available.
(v) Incorrect: a debit balance means the partner brings in cash (Bank A/c Dr. To Capital A/c).
Three statements are correct.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet shows 'Kunal's Loan ₹25,000'. Kunal is one of the partners. How is this loan treated while closing the books?
options: It is transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account along with creditors.
It is paid through Bank (Kunal's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c) after outside liabilities and before partners' capitals.
It is debited to the Realisation Account as a liability paid.
It is paid only after the capitals of all partners have been fully settled.
questions.explanation:
Section 48 sets the order of payment: first outside debts, then partners' loans (advances), then capitals, and finally any surplus.
A partner's loan is not an external liability, so it is not taken to the Realisation Account.
It is paid directly through Bank: Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
Option (4) reverses the legal order, because loans rank ahead of capital.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution, creditors of Rs 90,000 accept a building valued at Rs 1,20,000 in settlement of their claim and pay the difference to the firm in cash. What is the amount of the entry 'Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c' for this transaction?
options: Nil, as no entry is required
questions.explanation:
Given: Creditors' dues = Rs 90,000; value of building accepted = Rs 1,20,000.
Rule: If a creditor takes an asset worth more than his dues, he pays the excess to the firm. The entry is Bank Dr. To Realisation.
Calculation: Cash received = 1,20,000 − 90,000 = Rs 30,000.
The creditor and the building are both already in the Realisation Account, so only the cash is recorded.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Ritika was appointed to carry out the dissolution of her firm for a fixed remuneration of ₹20,000. She agreed to bear all realisation expenses. The actual expenses of ₹14,500 were paid by Ritika herself. What amount will be debited to the Realisation Account in respect of these items?
questions.explanation:
Given: remuneration ₹20,000; Ritika bears the expenses; actual expenses ₹14,500 paid by her.
Remuneration entry: Realisation A/c Dr. ₹20,000 To Ritika's Capital A/c ₹20,000.
The expenses are borne and paid by Ritika herself, so no entry is recorded for them.
So the amount debited to Realisation A/c = ₹20,000.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): No journal entry is passed when a creditor accepts an unrecorded investment in full settlement of his dues on dissolution of a firm.
Reason (R): Unrecorded assets are never shown in the Realisation Account, whatever way they are disposed of.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. When a creditor accepts any asset, recorded or unrecorded, in full and final settlement, NCERT requires no entry. The creditor's balance already stands on the credit side of Realisation Account and no cash moves.
R is false. An unrecorded asset that is sold or taken over by a partner is credited to Realisation Account. Examples are Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c, or Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Sundry debtors of Rs. 60,000 appear in the balance sheet with a Provision for Doubtful Debts of Rs. 3,000. On dissolution, the correct treatment in the Realisation Account is:
options: Debtors Rs. 57,000 debited; provision not shown
Debtors Rs. 60,000 debited and provision Rs. 3,000 credited
Debtors Rs. 60,000 credited and provision Rs. 3,000 debited
Debtors Rs. 60,000 debited; provision Rs. 3,000 transferred to partners' capital accounts
questions.explanation:
Step 1: NCERT states that sundry debtors are transferred to the Realisation Account at gross value. So Rs. 60,000 goes on the debit side.
Step 2: The provision for doubtful debts is transferred to the credit side along with the liabilities. So Rs. 3,000 is credited.
Step 3: Option (1) nets the two figures, which is not the prescribed method.
Step 4: Option (4) wrongly treats the provision like a reserve.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When a partner has agreed to bear realisation expenses and the firm pays them, Realisation Account is not debited with the expenses.
Reason (R): The expenses are the partner's personal burden, so the amount paid by the firm is debited to that partner's Capital Account.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. The firm does not bear these expenses, so they are not charged to Realisation Account.
R is true. The entry is Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c, because the firm paid on the partner's behalf.
R explains why A holds: the burden lies on the partner, not the firm.
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: In a partnership at will, how can the firm be dissolved without going to court?
options: Only with the written consent of all partners and the approval of the Registrar of Firms
Only on the expiry of a period fixed by the partners at the time of formation
By any one partner giving a notice in writing to the other partners, signifying the intention to dissolve the firm
Only by a majority decision of the partners recorded in the minutes
questions.explanation:
A partnership at will has no fixed term and no particular venture.
Such a firm may be dissolved by notice. Any one partner gives a written notice to the other partners stating that he or she intends to dissolve the firm.
Option (2) fails because a partnership at will has no fixed period. No majority vote or Registrar's approval is required.
Answer: (3)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Basis of distinction) with List-II (Position on dissolution of a FIRM):
List-I
A. Termination of business
B. Settlement of assets and liabilities
C. Economic relationship between partners
D. Books of account
List-II
(i) Comes to an end
(ii) Are closed
(iii) The firm's business is closed down
(iv) Assets are sold and liabilities are paid off
Choose the correct option.
options: A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(ii), D-(i)
A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii)
A-(i), B-(iv), C-(iii), D-(ii)
questions.explanation:
A-(iii): On dissolution of a firm, its business is closed.
B-(iv): Assets are sold and liabilities are paid off; they are not revalued.
C-(i): The economic relationship between the partners comes to an end.
D-(ii): The books of account are closed.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A loan given by the firm to a partner, shown on the assets side of the Balance Sheet, is not transferred to the Realisation Account on dissolution.
Reason (R): Such a loan is settled directly with the partner by recovering it from him; it is not sold in the market like other assets.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. The Realisation Account records only assets sold or taken over and external liabilities. A loan to a partner is kept out of it.
R is true. NCERT records recovery of the loan directly from the partner: Bank A/c Dr. To Loan to Partner A/c.
R explains A. The loan is not realised in the market, so it has no place in the Realisation Account.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When a partner is unable to contribute towards the debit balance of his capital account on dissolution, the amount not recoverable is borne by the solvent partners in the ratio of their capitals on the date of dissolution, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary.
Reason (R): A capital loss arising from the insolvency of a partner is shared by the solvent partners in their profit sharing ratio.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. This is the rule laid down in Garner vs. Murray. The deficiency of an insolvent partner is a capital loss, and it is borne by the solvent partners in the ratio of their capitals as on the date of dissolution.
R is false. Garner vs. Murray uses the capital ratio, not the profit sharing ratio, for this loss.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following journal entries on dissolution are correct?
(i) Expenses ₹6,500 paid by the firm: Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(ii) Partner agreed to bear expenses and paid them himself: Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
(iii) Partner agreed to bear expenses; firm paid them: Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iv) Partner gets remuneration ₹15,000, bears expenses and pays actual expenses of ₹11,800 himself: Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c ₹15,000 only
(v) Expenses paid by a partner on behalf of the firm: Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
questions.explanation:
(i) Correct: the firm's expense, paid in cash.
(ii) Incorrect: the partner bears and pays the expenses, so no entry is needed.
(iii) Correct: the firm paid on the partner's behalf, so his capital is debited.
(iv) Correct: only the remuneration is recorded. The expenses he bears and pays need no entry.
(v) Incorrect: the entry is reversed. It should be Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c.
Correct entries = 3.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: At the time of dissolution, a firm had a bank balance of ₹25,000. Assets were realised for ₹1,40,000. Creditors were paid ₹48,000 and realisation expenses of ₹2,000 were paid by the firm. A partner's loan of ₹15,000 was also repaid. No partner had a debit balance. What total amount will finally be paid to the partners on account of their capitals?
questions.explanation:
Given: opening bank ₹25,000; realisations ₹1,40,000; creditors ₹48,000; expenses ₹2,000; partner's loan ₹15,000.
Rule: the total finally paid to partners must equal the cash left in the bank account after all other payments.
Substituting: 25,000 + 1,40,000 − 48,000 − 2,000 − 15,000 = ₹1,00,000.
Option (2) wrongly ignores repayment of the partner's loan.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Neeraj was appointed to look after the dissolution work of his firm for a remuneration of ₹10,000. He agreed to bear realisation expenses up to ₹5,000. The actual realisation expenses of ₹8,200 were paid by Neeraj. What total amount will be credited to Neeraj's Capital Account in respect of remuneration and expenses?
questions.explanation:
Given: remuneration ₹10,000; Neeraj bears expenses up to ₹5,000; actual expenses ₹8,200 paid by him.
Remuneration entry: Realisation A/c Dr. To Neeraj's Capital A/c ₹10,000.
Excess borne by the firm: 8,200 − 5,000 = ₹3,200. Since Neeraj paid this excess on the firm's behalf: Realisation A/c Dr. To Neeraj's Capital A/c ₹3,200.
The ₹5,000 within his limit is his own burden, so no entry is made for it.
Total credited = 10,000 + 3,200 = ₹13,200.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following statements about entries on dissolution of a firm are correct?
(i) Creditors paid at a discount are recorded as Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c with the amount actually paid.
(ii) When a creditor accepts an asset worth more than his dues and pays the difference, Bank A/c is debited and Realisation A/c is credited.
(iii) When a creditor accepts an asset in full settlement, Creditors A/c is debited and the Asset A/c is credited.
(iv) When a partner takes over an asset, his Capital Account is credited.
(v) External liabilities are transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account.
questions.explanation:
(i) Correct: the actual cash paid is debited to Realisation.
(ii) Correct: the excess received from the creditor is brought into Bank and credited to Realisation.
(iii) Incorrect: no entry is passed, because both accounts are already closed through Realisation.
(iv) Incorrect: the partner's capital is debited, not credited.
(v) Correct: liabilities go to the credit side of Realisation.
Three statements are correct.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: During dissolution, a partner, Anubha, pays realisation expenses of ₹7,800 out of her own pocket on behalf of the firm. She has not agreed to bear these expenses. Which account is credited?
options: Bank Account
Realisation Account
Anubha's Capital Account
Anubha's Loan Account
questions.explanation:
The expense belongs to the firm, so Realisation Account is debited.
Anubha paid it on the firm's behalf, so the firm owes her ₹7,800. Her Capital Account is credited.
Entry: Realisation A/c Dr. To Anubha's Capital A/c.
Bank is not credited because the firm paid nothing. A Loan Account is not used for this.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Situation) with List-II (Mode of dissolution of the firm):
List-I
(A) A partner becomes an alien enemy after war is declared between his country and India
(B) A partner becomes of unsound mind and another partner files a suit
(C) A firm formed for 3 years completes its term
(D) All partners consent to close the firm
List-II
(i) Dissolution by court
(ii) Compulsory dissolution
(iii) Dissolution on happening of a contingency
(iv) Dissolution by agreement
options: A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iii), D-(iv)
A-(i), B-(ii), C-(iv), D-(iii)
A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(iv)
A-(iii), B-(i), C-(ii), D-(iv)
questions.explanation:
(A) A partner becoming an alien enemy makes it unlawful to carry on the business in partnership. This is compulsory dissolution: (ii).
(B) Insanity of a partner is a ground on which the court may order dissolution at the suit of a partner: (i).
(C) Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency: (iii).
(D) Consent of all partners is dissolution by agreement: (iv).
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: In which of the following situations are the books of account of the firm closed?
options: Change in the profit sharing ratio among existing partners
Admission of a new partner
Death of a partner, where the surviving partners continue the business
Dissolution of the firm by mutual agreement of all partners
questions.explanation:
The books of account are closed only when the business itself is terminated, which happens on dissolution of the firm.
A change in profit sharing ratio, an admission, or a death where the surviving partners carry on the business are cases of dissolution of partnership only. In each of these the business continues, so the books are not closed.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): If a contingent liability for bills discounted becomes payable during dissolution and the firm pays it, Realisation Account is debited.
Reason (R): Payment of an unrecorded liability by the firm is recorded by debiting Realisation Account and crediting Bank Account.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.explanation:
A is true: once the contingent liability becomes payable and is paid, it affects realisation.
R is true: the entry for paying an unrecorded liability is Realisation A/c Dr. to Bank A/c.
R correctly explains why Realisation Account is debited in A.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A partnership firm can be dissolved by an order of the court, whereas dissolution of partnership does not require the court's intervention.
Reason (R): The court can order dissolution of a firm only when all the partners jointly apply for it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. A firm may be dissolved by the court's order. Dissolution of partnership happens by mutual agreement without court intervention.
R is false. The court acts at the suit of even a single partner, on grounds such as insanity, misconduct or persistent breach of agreement. Consent of all partners is a separate mode, namely dissolution by agreement.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A creditor owed Rs 25,000 accepts furniture valued at Rs 18,000 and Rs 7,000 in cash. The only entry passed is Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c Rs 7,000.
Reason (R): The creditor's full claim is already on the credit side and the furniture is already on the debit side of the Realisation Account, so only the cash paid needs to be recorded.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. When an asset is accepted in part settlement, NCERT requires an entry only for the cash payment of Rs 7,000.
R is true. The creditor and the furniture were both already transferred to the Realisation Account, so the asset handover needs no entry.
R explains exactly why only the cash part is recorded.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the case and answer the question.
Kavya, Neel and Ishaan were partners in 'KNI Traders'. On March 31, 2025, Ishaan retired. Kavya and Neel decided to carry on the same business under the same name, 'KNI Traders', sharing profits equally.
Which of the following statements correctly describes this situation?
options: Both the partnership and the firm stand dissolved because a partner has left the business.
Only the partnership is dissolved. Assets and liabilities are revalued, a new balance sheet is drawn, and the books of the firm are not closed.
Only the firm is dissolved, while the partnership between Kavya and Neel continues unchanged.
The firm is compulsorily dissolved, so its assets must be sold and a Realisation Account prepared.
questions.explanation:
(1) Incorrect: the retirement of a partner dissolves the partnership, but the remaining partners may continue the firm.
(2) Correct: this is reconstitution. The existing relationship ends, but the business continues. Assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn, so the books are not closed.
(3) Incorrect: the firm cannot be dissolved without the partnership being dissolved, since dissolution of a firm always includes dissolution of partnership.
(4) Incorrect: retirement is not a ground for compulsory dissolution. A Realisation Account is prepared only when the firm itself is dissolved.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (items in the Balance Sheet at the time of dissolution) with List-II (treatment):
List-I
A. Furniture
B. Investment Fluctuation Fund
C. General Reserve
D. Partner's current account (credit balance)
List-II
(i) Credited to Realisation Account
(ii) Debited to Realisation Account at book value
(iii) Transferred to the respective partner's capital account
(iv) Credited to partners' capital accounts in profit sharing ratio
options: A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(iii)
A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii)
A-(i), B-(ii), C-(iv), D-(iii)
A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iii), D-(iv)
questions.explanation:
A. Furniture is an asset, so it is debited to Realisation A/c at book value: (ii).
B. Investment Fluctuation Fund appears on the credit side of Realisation A/c in Fig 4.1: (i).
C. General Reserve is an accumulated profit. It is credited to partners' capital accounts in profit sharing ratio: (iv).
D. A partner's current account is not taken to Realisation A/c. Its balance goes to that partner's capital account: (iii).
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Paras and Priya dissolved their firm. Assets (other than cash) of book value Rs. 2,00,000 and creditors of Rs. 50,000 were transferred to Realisation Account. Further information:
1. Assets realised Rs. 1,90,000; creditors were paid Rs. 48,000.
2. Rs. 1,500 was recovered from debtors written off as bad in the previous year.
3. An old typewriter, fully written off, was estimated to realise Rs. 400 and was taken by Priya at the estimated price less 25%.
4. 100 shares of Rs. 10 each, fully written off earlier, were valued at Rs. 6 each and divided among the partners.
5. A contingent liability for bills discounted materialised, and Rs. 4,000 was paid.
6. An electricity bill of Rs. 2,500, not recorded, was paid.
7. Realisation expenses of Rs. 1,800 were paid by the firm.
What is the result on realisation?
options: Loss Rs. 13,900
Loss Rs. 15,400
Loss Rs. 7,400
Loss Rs. 14,800
questions.explanation:
Credit side of Realisation Account:
- Creditors: 50,000
- Assets realised: 1,90,000
- Bad debts recovered: 1,500
- Typewriter taken by Priya: 400 × 75% = 300
- Shares taken by partners: 100 × 6 = 600
- Total: Rs. 2,42,400

Debit side of Realisation Account:
- Assets: 2,00,000
- Creditors paid: 48,000
- Bills discounted paid: 4,000
- Electricity bill paid: 2,500
- Expenses: 1,800
- Total: Rs. 2,56,300

Loss = 2,56,300 − 2,42,400 = Rs. 13,900.
Option (2) wrongly ignores the bad debts recovered.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution, the firm's creditors total Rs 80,000.
- One creditor, owed Rs 20,000, accepts an unrecorded computer valued at Rs 14,000 and is paid Rs 6,000 in cash in full settlement.
- The remaining creditors are paid in cash at a discount of 10%.
What total amount will be debited to the Realisation Account for payment to creditors?
questions.explanation:
Rule: when a creditor accepts an asset as part payment, an entry is made only for the cash paid. No entry is made for the unrecorded computer.
Cash to the first creditor = Rs 6,000.
Remaining creditors = 80,000 - 20,000 = Rs 60,000. Paid at 10% discount = Rs 54,000.
Total debited (Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c) = 6,000 + 54,000 = Rs 60,000.
Adding the computer's value would wrongly give Rs 74,000.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of the firm of Kavya and Rehan, ₹1,50,000 was available after realising all assets. Outside creditors of ₹90,000 were paid in full. Kavya had given the firm a loan of ₹50,000 and Rehan a loan of ₹30,000. How much will Kavya receive towards her loan?
questions.explanation:
Given: cash available ₹1,50,000; creditors ₹90,000; partners' loans: Kavya ₹50,000, Rehan ₹30,000.
Rule: outside debts are paid first. Partners' loans are then paid proportionately if the balance is not enough.
Balance after creditors = 1,50,000 − 90,000 = ₹60,000, which is less than the total loans of ₹80,000.
Kavya's share = 60,000 × 50,000/80,000 = ₹37,500.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: The firm of Arjun and Neel is dissolved, and its assets are insufficient to pay its creditors. Arjun has private assets of ₹2,00,000 and private liabilities of ₹1,40,000. His wife owns jewellery worth ₹80,000. Under Section 49, what is the maximum amount Arjun's private estate can make available towards the firm's debts?
questions.explanation:
Given: private assets ₹2,00,000; private liabilities ₹1,40,000; wife's jewellery ₹80,000.
Rule (Sec 49): private property is applied first to private debts. Only the surplus can go towards firm's debts.
The wife's personal property is not part of the partner's private property, so it is excluded.
Surplus = 2,00,000 − 1,40,000 = ₹60,000.
Option (2) wrongly includes the wife's jewellery.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: In a partnership at will, which of the following correctly describes how the firm may be dissolved by notice?
options: All partners must jointly apply to the court for dissolution
Any one partner gives a written notice to the other partners stating that he intends to seek dissolution of the firm
Any one partner gives an oral notice to the Registrar of Firms
A notice can be given only by the partner with the largest capital
questions.explanation:
Under dissolution by notice, a partnership at will may be dissolved if any one partner gives notice in writing to the other partners.
The notice must state his intention to seek dissolution of the firm.
No court application is required, so (a) is wrong.
The notice goes to the other partners, not to the Registrar, and it must be in writing, so (c) is wrong.
Any partner may give it, whatever his capital, so (d) is wrong.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of dissolution of a partnership firm but NOT of dissolution of partnership?
options: Assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn
Economic relationship among partners continues in a changed form
The books of account are closed
It takes place on admission of a new partner
questions.explanation:
On dissolution of a firm, the business itself is closed. Assets are sold, liabilities are paid and the books of account are closed.
On dissolution of partnership, the business continues. Assets and liabilities are only revalued and the economic relationship continues in a changed form.
Options (1), (2) and (4) all describe dissolution of partnership, for example on admission of a partner.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
The liabilities side of the balance sheet of Ravi and Raman on the date of dissolution shows:
Creditors Rs. 40,000; Bills payable Rs. 10,000; Mrs. Ravi's loan Rs. 15,000; Ravi's loan Rs. 20,000; Investment Fluctuation Fund Rs. 3,000; Provision for doubtful debts Rs. 1,500; Provision for depreciation on furniture Rs. 4,000; General Reserve Rs. 12,000; Raman's current account Rs. 5,000; Capitals Rs. 1,00,000.
What amount will be credited to the Realisation Account when the liabilities are transferred?
questions.explanation:
Given: Only external liabilities, provisions and the Investment Fluctuation Fund are transferred.
Include: Creditors 40,000 + Bills payable 10,000 + Mrs. Ravi's loan 15,000 + Investment Fluctuation Fund 3,000 + Provision for doubtful debts 1,500 + Provision for depreciation 4,000.
Exclude: Ravi's loan (partner), General Reserve and current account (both go to capital), and capitals.
Substituting: 40,000 + 10,000 + 15,000 + 3,000 + 1,500 + 4,000 = 73,500.
So the amount credited = Rs. 73,500.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On the dissolution of a firm, realisation expenses of ₹6,500 were paid by the firm. No partner has agreed to bear them. Which journal entry records this?
options: Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c ₹6,500
Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank A/c ₹6,500
Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c ₹6,500
Realisation A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs ₹6,500
questions.explanation:
Realisation expenses are a cost of winding up the firm, so they are charged to Realisation Account.
The firm paid them, so Bank Account is credited.
Entry: Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c ₹6,500.
Option (2) would apply only if a partner had agreed to bear the expenses.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: P and Q share profits in the ratio 3:1. On dissolution, the firm's assets realised ₹3,00,000. Outside creditors were ₹80,000. P had given the firm a loan of ₹20,000. Capital balances (after all adjustments, before distributing any surplus) were P ₹1,00,000 and Q ₹60,000. What is the TOTAL amount P will receive from the firm?
questions.explanation:
Given: realised ₹3,00,000; creditors ₹80,000; P's loan ₹20,000; capitals P ₹1,00,000, Q ₹60,000; ratio 3:1.
Step 1: pay creditors: 3,00,000 − 80,000 = ₹2,20,000 left.
Step 2: repay P's loan: 2,20,000 − 20,000 = ₹2,00,000 left.
Step 3: repay capitals of ₹1,60,000: residue = ₹40,000.
Step 4: share the residue 3:1, so P gets ₹30,000.
P's total = 20,000 + 1,00,000 + 30,000 = ₹1,50,000.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Kabir, a partner, is appointed to look after the dissolution work for a remuneration of Rs 10,000 and he agrees to bear all realisation expenses. The actual realisation expenses of Rs 6,000 are paid by the firm. Which set of entries is correct?
options: Realisation A/c Dr. To Kabir's Capital A/c Rs 10,000; and Kabir's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c Rs 6,000
Realisation A/c Dr. Rs 16,000 To Kabir's Capital A/c Rs 10,000 and To Bank A/c Rs 6,000
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c Rs 6,000; and Realisation A/c Dr. To Kabir's Capital A/c Rs 10,000
Kabir's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c Rs 4,000
questions.explanation:
The agreed remuneration is a realisation cost of the firm, so Realisation A/c is debited and Kabir's Capital A/c credited with Rs 10,000.
Kabir has agreed to bear the expenses. So when the firm pays them, the Rs 6,000 is charged to his capital: Kabir's Capital Dr. To Bank.
Options (2) and (3) wrongly charge the Rs 6,000 to the Realisation Account a second time.
Net effect: Realisation A/c bears Rs 10,000, and Kabir's capital gains a net Rs 4,000.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
The assets side of the balance sheet of a firm on the date of dissolution shows:
Cash in hand Rs. 12,000; Bank Rs. 18,000; Sundry debtors Rs. 50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts Rs. 2,000; Stock Rs. 30,000; Machinery Rs. 60,000; Investments Rs. 25,000; Profit and Loss Account (debit balance) Rs. 8,000.
What is the total of assets transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account?
questions.explanation:
Given: Cash, bank and the fictitious debit balance of Profit and Loss are excluded. Debtors are taken at gross value.
Formula: Assets transferred = Debtors (gross) + Stock + Machinery + Investments.
Substituting: 50,000 + 30,000 + 60,000 + 25,000 = 1,65,000.
Check: Rs. 1,63,000 uses net debtors. Rs. 1,73,000 wrongly includes Profit and Loss. Rs. 1,95,000 wrongly includes cash and bank.
So the total debited = Rs. 1,65,000.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: While winding up, a firm pays a repair bill that was not recorded in its books. Which statement is correct?
options: The payment is debited to the partners’ capital accounts.
The bill is ignored because it was not recorded earlier.
The payment is credited to Realisation Account.
The payment is debited to Realisation Account.
questions.explanation:
The unpaid repair bill is an unrecorded liability that the firm has settled.
Realisation Account is debited for the payment and Bank Account is credited. It cannot be ignored merely because it was previously unrecorded.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Statement I: In a Realisation Account the assets are actually sold and the liabilities paid off, whereas in a Revaluation Account only the changes in the values of assets and liabilities are recorded and a new balance sheet is drawn.
Statement II: A Revaluation Account is prepared on dissolution of the firm, while a Realisation Account is prepared on reconstitution such as admission or retirement of a partner.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct. On dissolution of a firm, assets are sold and liabilities paid. On dissolution of partnership (reconstitution), assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn.
Statement II is incorrect because it reverses the two accounts. The Revaluation Account belongs to reconstitution, when the business continues. The Realisation Account belongs to dissolution of the firm, when the books are closed.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Kavya is to look after the dissolution work for a remuneration of ₹10,000. She has agreed to bear dissolution expenses up to ₹5,000. Actual expenses of ₹6,200 were paid by Kavya herself. What total amount will be credited to Kavya's Capital Account through Realisation Account?
questions.explanation:
Given: remuneration ₹10,000; Kavya bears expenses up to ₹5,000; actual expenses ₹6,200, paid by Kavya.
Remuneration: Realisation A/c Dr. To Kavya's Capital A/c ₹10,000.
The excess expense is the firm's burden: 6,200 − 5,000 = ₹1,200. Realisation A/c Dr. To Kavya's Capital A/c ₹1,200.
The ₹5,000 she bears and pays herself needs no entry.
Total credited = 10,000 + 1,200 = ₹11,200.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the case and answer:
Arjun, Bela and Chirag were partners in 'ABC Traders', sharing profits 2:2:1. On 31 March, Chirag retired. Arjun and Bela decided to continue the business under the same name, sharing profits equally. They did not approach any court.
Which of the following correctly describes the position?
options: The firm is dissolved because one partner has left, so all assets must be sold
Only the partnership is dissolved; the firm continues, assets and liabilities are revalued, and no court intervention is required
The firm is dissolved by court, since retirement can take effect only through a court order
Neither the partnership nor the firm is dissolved, since the firm's name is unchanged
questions.explanation:
Retirement of a partner is a mode of dissolution of partnership, i.e. reconstitution. The relationship among the existing partners changes.
The relationship has not ended among all partners, so the firm is not dissolved. It can continue under the same name.
In such a case, assets and liabilities are revalued and no court intervention is needed, since this is a mutual arrangement.
Option (4) fails because a partnership is dissolved even when the name is kept.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the statements regarding settlement of accounts on dissolution of a firm:
Statement I: After paying third-party debts, a partner's loan to the firm is repaid before the partners' capitals are returned.
Statement II: In the absence of an agreement, the deficiency of an insolvent partner is borne by the solvent partners in their profit sharing ratio.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct. Section 48 applies assets first to outside debts, then to partners' advances or loans, then to capital, and finally the residue in the profit sharing ratio.
Statement II is incorrect. Under Garner vs. Murray, solvent partners bear such a capital loss in the ratio of their capitals on the date of dissolution, not in the profit sharing ratio.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): If the firm's assets are not sufficient to pay off its outside liabilities on dissolution, the partners have to contribute out of their private assets.
Reason (R): Under Section 48, losses including deficiencies of capital are met lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true: when the firm's assets fall short, partners contribute from their net private assets (private assets minus private liabilities).
R is true: Section 48(a) makes losses payable from profits, then capital, and lastly by the partners individually in profit-sharing ratio.
R explains why partners must bring in money from outside the firm, so R correctly explains A.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: When only the partnership is dissolved (for example, on admission of a partner), the firm's assets and liabilities are:
options: Revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn up
Sold and liabilities are paid off
Transferred to a Realisation Account
Distributed among partners in their capital ratio
questions.explanation:
On dissolution of partnership, the business continues. Assets and liabilities are therefore revalued and a new balance sheet is prepared.
Selling assets and paying liabilities, and recording these through a Realisation Account, happen only on dissolution of the firm.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, the stock appeared in the books at Rs 1,20,000. A partner, Kunal, took over 40% of the stock at a discount of 15% on book value. The remaining stock was sold at a profit of 25% on cost. What total amount will be credited to the Realisation Account in respect of stock (by Kunal's Capital Account and by Bank Account together)?
questions.explanation:
Given: book value of stock is Rs 1,20,000.
Kunal's portion: 40% of 1,20,000 = Rs 48,000. Less 15% discount, so $48{,}000 \times 0.85$ = Rs 40,800, credited through Kunal's Capital A/c.
Remaining stock: Rs 72,000. Profit of 25% on cost gives $72{,}000 \times 1.25$ = Rs 90,000, credited through Bank A/c.
Total credit = 40,800 + 90,000 = Rs 1,30,800.
Rs 1,36,800 wrongly treats the 25% as profit on the sale price.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: At the time of dissolution, a firm's bank balance was Rs 20,000. Assets realised Rs 1,50,000. Creditors were paid Rs 58,000 and realisation expenses of Rs 2,000 were paid by the firm. A partner's loan of Rs 15,000 was also repaid. No partner's capital shows a debit balance. What total amount will finally be paid to the partners on their capital accounts?
questions.explanation:
Given: Opening bank Rs 20,000; realisations Rs 1,50,000; payments Rs 58,000 + 2,000 + 15,000.
Formula: The amount payable to partners must equal the cash left after all other payments.
Substituting: 20,000 + 1,50,000 − 58,000 − 2,000 − 15,000 = Rs 95,000.
So the partners receive Rs 95,000 in total. Option (1) wrongly treats the partner's loan as part of the capital payment.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On dissolution of a firm, General Reserve appearing in the Balance Sheet is not transferred to the Realisation Account but is credited to the partners' capital accounts.
Reason (R): General Reserve represents profits of earlier years that have not been distributed, and these profits belong to the partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. The Realisation Account receives only assets (other than cash, bank and fictitious assets) and external liabilities. General Reserve is neither of these.
The entry is: General Reserve A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs.
R is true. A reserve is undistributed past profit, so it belongs to the partners and is shared in their profit-sharing ratio.
R explains why the reserve goes to the capital accounts rather than to the Realisation Account.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Arjun, Bela and Chirag are partners. Chirag retires on March 31, and Arjun and Bela decide to carry on the business under the same firm name. Which of the following correctly describes the accounting position?
options: A Realisation Account is opened, all assets are sold and the books are closed
The firm is dissolved compulsorily, and a court order is needed to continue
Assets and liabilities are revalued, a new balance sheet is drawn, and the business continues
The economic relationship of all three partners ends, and the business is wound up
questions.explanation:
Chirag's retirement dissolves the partnership, but the firm continues because Arjun and Bela carry on the business.
In such a case, assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is prepared. There is no Realisation Account, no sale of all assets and no closing of books.
No court order is needed, since this is not compulsory dissolution.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Case: Mehul and Nisha share profits 2:1. Their Balance Sheet on dissolution showed:
Liabilities: Creditors ₹36,000; Nisha's Loan ₹10,000; Mrs. Mehul's Loan ₹15,000; General Reserve ₹9,000; Capitals: Mehul ₹50,000, Nisha ₹30,000.
Assets: Bank ₹14,000; Debtors ₹40,000; Stock ₹30,000; Machinery ₹66,000.
Terms: Mehul agreed to pay Mrs. Mehul's loan. Debtors realised ₹38,000. Nisha took over stock at ₹27,000. Machinery was sold for ₹70,000. Creditors accepted ₹35,000. Realisation expenses of ₹3,000 were paid by the firm.
What amount is finally paid to Mehul?
questions.explanation:
Realisation Dr.: assets 1,36,000 + Mehul (wife's loan) 15,000 + creditors paid 35,000 + expenses 3,000 = ₹1,89,000.
Realisation Cr.: creditors 36,000 + Mrs. Mehul's loan 15,000 + Nisha (stock) 27,000 + cash from assets 1,08,000 = ₹1,86,000.
Loss = ₹3,000, of which Mehul's share is 2,000.
Mehul's capital = 50,000 + reserve 6,000 + wife's loan 15,000 − loss 2,000 = ₹69,000.
Check: Nisha receives 30,000 + 3,000 − 27,000 − 1,000 = 5,000. Bank = 14,000 + 1,08,000 − 35,000 − 3,000 − 10,000 = 74,000 = 69,000 + 5,000.
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: While closing its books, a firm pays ₹3,250 as employee compensation and ₹1,750 for an outstanding electricity bill. Neither liability was recorded earlier. What is the total debit to Realisation Account for these payments?
questions.explanation:
Given: Employee compensation paid is ₹3,250 and the outstanding electricity bill paid is ₹1,750.
Both are liabilities settled by the firm, so each payment is debited to Realisation Account.
Substituting: Total debit = ₹3,250 + ₹1,750 = ₹5,000.
Answer: (4)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the statements:
Statement I: The court generally intervenes to bring about dissolution of a partnership, such as on the retirement of a partner.
Statement II: In dissolution of partnership, the economic relationship between the partners continues, though in a changed form.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Statement I is incorrect. Dissolution of partnership happens by mutual agreement, so the court does not intervene. Only a firm can be dissolved by the court's order.
Statement II is correct. The business continues, and the partners remain economically related under the new arrangement.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Partners A and B share profits in the ratio of 3:2. On dissolution, A takes over unrecorded goodwill for ₹12,000, the firm recovers ₹3,000 from a debt written off earlier, and it pays ₹5,000 on a materialised bills-discounted liability and ₹4,000 as employee compensation. If these are the only Realisation Account items, how much realisation profit is credited to A’s capital account?
questions.explanation:
Given: Goodwill taken over and bad-debt recovery credit Realisation Account by ₹12,000 and ₹3,000. The two liability payments debit it by ₹5,000 and ₹4,000.
Profit on realisation = ₹12,000 + ₹3,000 − ₹5,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹6,000.
A receives 3/5 of this profit: ₹6,000 × 3/5 = ₹3,600.
Answer: (3)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Dissolution of a partnership firm necessarily involves dissolution of partnership.
Reason (R): On dissolution of a firm, the relationship between all the partners comes to an end and the business is closed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. Section 39 defines dissolution of the firm as dissolution of partnership between all the partners. So the partnership also ends.
R is true. The firm stops business except for winding up, and the economic relationship of all partners ends.
R explains A: since every partner's relationship ends, the partnership itself must also end.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Statement I: When a partner agrees to discharge a liability of the firm on dissolution, the entry is Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c.
Statement II: The partner's capital is credited because the partner settles the firm's obligation from his own resources, so the firm now owes him that amount.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct. Paying a liability is a debit to Realisation. Here the partner pays it instead of the firm, so the credit goes to his Capital Account and not to Bank.
Statement II is correct. The partner meets the firm's debt personally, which increases the amount the firm must pay him. Hence his capital is credited.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Case: Ashok, Babu and Chetan share profits in the proportion $\frac{1}{2}:\frac{1}{3}:\frac{1}{6}$. They dissolve their firm with the following details:
- Assets other than bank (including debtors at their gross value) are transferred to the Realisation Account at Rs 3,00,000.
- The Balance Sheet also shows a Provision for Doubtful Debts of Rs 4,000, Creditors of Rs 80,000 and a Workmen Compensation Reserve of Rs 18,000.
- The assets realised Rs 3,00,000 and creditors were paid Rs 78,000.
- An office computer not recorded in the books realised Rs 9,000.
- Realisation expenses of Rs 3,000 were paid by the firm.
- There is no claim against the Workmen Compensation Reserve.
What total amount will be credited to Chetan's Capital Account on account of the realisation profit and the Workmen Compensation Reserve?
questions.explanation:
Debit side of Realisation A/c: assets 3,00,000 + creditors paid 78,000 + expenses 3,000 = Rs 3,81,000.
Credit side: creditors 80,000 + provision 4,000 + assets realised 3,00,000 + unrecorded computer 9,000 = Rs 3,93,000.
Profit on realisation = Rs 12,000. The ratio $\frac{1}{2}:\frac{1}{3}:\frac{1}{6}$ equals 3:2:1, so Chetan gets $\frac{1}{6}$ = Rs 2,000.
The Workmen Compensation Reserve has no claim, so it is credited in full to capitals. Chetan gets $18{,}000 \times \frac{1}{6}$ = Rs 3,000.
Total credited to Chetan = Rs 5,000. Rs 3,500 results from ignoring the unrecorded computer.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Statement I: When a partner retires and the remaining partners continue the business, the books of account of the firm must be closed.
Statement II: On dissolution of partnership, the economic relationship between the partners continues, though in a changed form.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Statement I is incorrect. Retirement causes only dissolution of partnership. The business is not terminated, so the books are not closed.
Statement II is correct. On dissolution of partnership, the economic relationship among the partners continues in a changed form.
That relationship ends only on dissolution of the firm.
Answer: (4)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: A customer pays a debt that the firm had written off as bad in the previous year. On dissolution, which account is credited for the amount recovered?
options: Realisation Account
Customer’s Account
Partners’ Capital Accounts
Provision for Doubtful Debts Account
questions.explanation:
The debt was written off earlier, so it is no longer a recorded debtor balance.
Its recovery brings cash into the firm: Bank Account is debited and Realisation Account is credited.
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (situation on dissolution) with List-II (journal entry):
List-I
(A) Realisation expenses paid by the firm
(B) Partner agreed to bear expenses; firm paid them
(C) Remuneration allowed to a partner for dissolution work
(D) Partner agreed to bear expenses and paid them himself
List-II
(i) Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(ii) No entry
(iii) Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iv) Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
options: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(iv), B-(i), C-(iii), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(ii), C-(iv), D-(i)
questions.explanation:

(B) The firm pays an amount that the partner is liable for, so it is charged to him: Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c, so (i).
(C) The remuneration is a cost of dissolution owed to the partner: Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c, so (iv).
(D) The partner bears and pays the expenses himself, so no entry is made: (ii).
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Pari, Qasim and Ravi are partners. Qasim transfers the whole of his interest in the firm to an outsider. On a suit filed by Pari, the court orders the firm to be dissolved. Which of the following correctly describes the consequences?
options: Assets are revalued, Pari and Ravi continue the business, and only Qasim's capital account is closed
Assets are sold and liabilities paid off, the economic relationship among all partners ends, and the books are closed
Assets are sold, but Pari and Ravi continue the business with the same books of account
Only the partnership is dissolved, because a dissolution ordered by court cannot dissolve the firm
questions.explanation:
Transfer of the whole of a partner's interest to a third party is a ground on which the court may order dissolution of the firm.
Once the firm is dissolved, its business is terminated. Assets are sold, liabilities are paid off, the relationship among all partners ends and the books are closed.
Option (1) describes dissolution of partnership, not dissolution of the firm.
Option (4) is wrong because the court can order dissolution of the firm.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (transaction on dissolution) with List-II (journal entry):
List-I
(A) Creditors of Rs. 90,000 accept a building valued at Rs. 1,20,000 and pay Rs. 30,000 to the firm
(B) A creditor of Rs. 10,000 accepts equipment worth Rs. 8,000 and Rs. 2,000 in cash
(C) A creditor accepts an asset in full and final settlement of his dues
(D) A partner agrees to discharge a creditor of the firm
List-II
(i) Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c (Rs. 2,000)
(ii) No entry
(iii) Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
(iv) Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c (Rs. 30,000)
options: A-(i), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(iii)
A-(iv), B-(ii), C-(i), D-(iii)
A-(iii), B-(i), C-(ii), D-(iv)
A-(iv), B-(i), C-(ii), D-(iii)
questions.explanation:
(A) The creditor pays the excess of asset value over his dues, so cash comes in: Bank Dr. To Realisation (iv).
(B) Only the cash part of the payment is recorded: Realisation Dr. To Bank Rs. 2,000 (i).
(C) Both the asset and the creditor are already in the Realisation A/c and no cash moves, so no entry is needed (ii).
(D) The partner assumes the liability, so his capital account is credited: Realisation Dr. To Partner's Capital (iii).

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following journal entries on dissolution of a firm is INCORRECT?
options: A creditor accepts a machine in full settlement of his dues: no entry
An unrecorded asset is taken over by a partner: Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
A loan given by a partner to the firm is closed: Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
A partner agrees to pay a liability of the firm: Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
questions.explanation:
(1) Correct: when a creditor accepts an asset in full settlement, no entry is passed.
(2) Correct: the partner's capital is debited and Realisation is credited for the asset taken over.
(4) Correct: a liability assumed by a partner is debited to Realisation and credited to his Capital.
(3) Incorrect: a partner's loan to the firm is not transferred to the Realisation Account. It is paid off directly: Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On dissolution of a firm, a loan given by a partner to the firm is not transferred to the Realisation Account.
Reason (R): Only external (third-party) liabilities are transferred to the credit of the Realisation Account.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. A partner's loan is an internal liability. It is paid directly (Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c) after the outside liabilities are paid.
R is true. Under NCERT, all external liabilities, including provisions, are credited to the Realisation Account.
R explains A, because the partner's loan is not an external liability.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Dissolution of partnership does not necessarily involve dissolution of the firm
After dissolution of a firm, no business is carried on except the activities related to winding up its affairs
Since a firm may continue its business after the death of a partner, the death of a partner does not dissolve even the partnership
A partnership formed for a particular venture is dissolved on completion of that venture
questions.explanation:
(1) Correct: a firm may continue after reconstitution.
(2) Correct: after dissolution, only winding up (sale of assets, payment of liabilities, settling partners' claims) is permitted.
(3) Incorrect: death of a partner always dissolves the partnership, because the existing relationship changes. Only the firm may continue if the remaining partners so decide.
(4) Correct: completion of the venture is a listed mode of dissolution of partnership.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The firm of Xavier, Yash and Zoya is compulsorily dissolved when Xavier and Yash are declared insolvent, even though Zoya remains solvent.
Reason (R): When all the partners or all but one partner become insolvent, they become incompetent to sign a contract.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. In a three-partner firm, two insolvent partners means 'all but one' partner is insolvent, which causes compulsory dissolution.
R is true. NCERT gives the reason: insolvent partners become incompetent to sign a contract.
This incapacity is exactly why the law dissolves the firm compulsorily, so R explains A.
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, assets (other than cash) of book value Rs. 1,20,000 and creditors of Rs. 40,000 were transferred to the Realisation Account. The assets realised Rs. 1,10,000. Creditors were paid at a 5% discount. Realisation expenses of Rs. 3,000 were paid by the firm. An unrecorded asset was taken over by a partner at Rs. 4,000. What is the result on realisation?
options: Loss Rs. 7,000
Loss Rs. 11,000
Loss Rs. 9,000
Loss Rs. 4,000
questions.explanation:
Given: assets Rs. 1,20,000; creditors Rs. 40,000, paid Rs. 38,000 after the 5% discount.
Debit side: 1,20,000 + 38,000 (creditors paid) + 3,000 (expenses) = Rs. 1,61,000.
Credit side: 40,000 (creditors) + 1,10,000 (assets realised) + 4,000 (unrecorded asset taken by partner) = Rs. 1,54,000.
So, Loss = 1,61,000 − 1,54,000 = Rs. 7,000. Ignoring the unrecorded asset would wrongly give Rs. 11,000.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following statements about modes of dissolution of a firm is INCORRECT?
options: A firm constituted for a fixed term is dissolved on expiry of that term, subject to the contract between the partners
Dissolution by court takes place at the suit of a partner
A firm may be dissolved without the intervention of a court
Any partner of a firm, including one constituted for a fixed term, may dissolve it by giving a written notice to the other partners
questions.explanation:
(a) Correct: expiry of a fixed term is a contingency, subject to contract.
(b) Correct: the court orders dissolution 'at the suit of a partner'.
(c) Correct: dissolution by agreement, compulsory dissolution, contingencies and notice all work without a court.
(d) Incorrect: dissolution by notice is available only in a partnership at will, not in a fixed-term partnership.
Answer: (4)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Dissolution of a firm necessarily brings about dissolution of the partnership.
Reason (R): Dissolution of a firm means discontinuance of the relationship between all the partners of the firm.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. NCERT states that dissolution of the firm necessarily brings in dissolution of the partnership, but the reverse is not necessarily true.
R is true. Under Section 39, dissolution of a firm is the breaking of the relationship among all partners.
If the relationship among all partners ends, the partnership itself must end. So R correctly explains A.
Answer: (1)

(A) Repayment of a partner's loan to the firm

(C) A partner brings cash to clear the debit balance in his capital account

(ii) Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iii) Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
(iv) Bank A/c Dr. To Loan to Partner A/c

A-(iii), B-(ii), C-(iv), D-(i)

A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(ii)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following lead to dissolution of partnership only, with the firm continuing its business?
(a) Change in the existing profit sharing ratio
(b) Admission of a new partner
(c) The business of the firm becomes illegal
(d) Retirement of a partner
(e) All partners except one become insolvent
(f) Death of a partner, the surviving partners agreeing to carry on the business
options: Three
Four
Five
Two
questions.explanation:
(a), (b) and (d) are correct. Each is a reconstitution of the firm, so the business continues.
(f) is correct. The surviving partners continue, so only the partnership is dissolved.
(c) and (e) are not. Both are grounds for compulsory dissolution of the firm.
Count = 4.
