questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Cash in hand and bank balance are not transferred to the Realisation Account on dissolution of a firm.
Reason (R): Cash and bank balances need not be realised; they are the means through which the sale of assets and payment of liabilities are recorded.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. NCERT excludes cash in hand, bank balance and fictitious assets from the Realisation A/c.
R is true. The Realisation A/c works out the profit or loss on converting assets into cash. Cash is already in that form, and it is the account used for receipts and payments.
R therefore explains why cash and bank are kept out.

questions.question:
On dissolution, how many of the following items will be transferred to the Realisation Account?

(ii) Provision for doubtful debts
(iii) Bank overdraft
(iv) Partner's loan (shown on the liabilities side)
(v) General reserve
(vi) Cash in hand

(vi) Not transferred. Cash and bank are excluded.
(vii) Transferred. A loan from a partner's wife is an outside liability.

questions.question:

(A) Compulsory dissolution

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Vibha is appointed to look after the dissolution work for an agreed remuneration of ₹12,000. Which entry records the remuneration?
options: Vibha's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
Realisation A/c Dr. To Vibha's Capital A/c
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Vibha's Capital A/c
questions.explanation:
Remuneration for dissolution work is a cost of realisation, so Realisation Account is debited.
The amount is due to Vibha, so her Capital Account is credited.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution, a firm's stock (book value Rs 80,000) has been transferred to the Realisation Account. Partner Rekha takes over 40% of the stock at 15% less than its book value. The remaining stock is sold for cash at a profit of 25% on cost. What total amount is credited to the Realisation Account in respect of stock?
questions.explanation:
Given: Stock = Rs 80,000.
Stock taken by Rekha: 40% × 80,000 = 32,000. Agreed value = 32,000 × 0.85 = Rs 27,200. Entry: Rekha's Capital Dr. To Realisation.
Stock sold: 80,000 − 32,000 = 48,000. Sale price = 48,000 × 1.25 = Rs 60,000. Entry: Bank Dr. To Realisation.
Total credited to Realisation = 27,200 + 60,000 = Rs 87,200.
Option (4) ignores the 15% reduction on Rekha's share.
Answer: (1)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, sundry creditors of Rs. 50,000 are paid off at a discount of 4%. With what amount will the Realisation Account be debited for this payment?
questions.explanation:
Given: Creditors = Rs. 50,000; discount = 4%.
Formula: Amount paid = Creditors × (1 − discount rate).
Substituting: 50,000 × 0.96 = 48,000.
The entry is Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c, recorded at the amount actually paid, Rs. 48,000.
The discount of Rs. 2,000 needs no separate entry. It shows up automatically in the realisation profit, because creditors were credited at Rs. 50,000.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Sundry creditors of Rs 40,000 were transferred to the Realisation Account. On dissolution they were paid in cash at a discount of 5%. With what amount will the entry 'Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c' be recorded?
questions.explanation:
Given: Creditors = Rs 40,000; discount = 5%.
Rule: Payment of a liability is recorded at the amount actually paid (Realisation Dr. To Bank).
Calculation: Amount paid = 40,000 × 95% = Rs 38,000.
The discount of Rs 2,000 needs no separate entry. It shows up as part of the realisation profit.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Raghav and Ishan run a firm trading in a chemical. The Government later bans all trade in that chemical. What happens to the firm?
options: It continues until the partners mutually agree to close it
It is compulsorily dissolved because its business has become illegal
It can be dissolved only if a partner files a suit in court
It is dissolved only if the partnership deed specifically provides for such a ban
questions.explanation:
Compulsory dissolution occurs when the business of the firm becomes illegal.
The Government ban makes the trade unlawful. The firm is therefore dissolved by law. It does not depend on the partners' consent, the deed or a court order.
Option (1) is tempting, but an illegal business cannot continue even if the partners wish it to.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following events results in dissolution of the partnership but does NOT by itself dissolve the firm?
options: The business of the firm becomes illegal
All the partners become insolvent
Retirement of a partner, with the remaining partners continuing the business
The court orders dissolution because a partner has become insane
questions.explanation:
Retirement changes the existing relationship among partners, so the partnership is dissolved. The remaining partners may still carry on the business, so the firm continues.
If the business becomes illegal, or if all partners become insolvent, the firm is compulsorily dissolved.
A court order on the ground of a partner's insanity also dissolves the firm.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following are grounds on which a court may order dissolution of a firm at the suit of a partner?
(i) A partner becomes insane
(ii) A partner transfers the whole of his interest in the firm to a third party
(iii) The fixed term of the partnership expires
(iv) The business can be carried on only at a loss
(v) A partner dies
(vi) A partner persistently commits breach of the partnership agreement
questions.explanation:
(i) Court ground: insanity of a partner.
(ii) Court ground: transfer of the whole interest to a third party.
(iii) Not a court ground. Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency.
(iv) Court ground: business can be carried on only at a loss.
(v) Not a court ground. Death of a partner is a contingency.
(vi) Court ground: persistent breach of the agreement.
So there are 4 court grounds.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Partner P of a dissolved firm owes private debts, and the firm's liabilities exceed its assets. Which of the following statements is correct under Section 49 of the Partnership Act, 1932?
options: Firm's property is applied first to P's private debts and then to the firm's debts
P's private property is applied first to his private debts, and only the surplus may be used for the firm's debts
Personal property of P's wife can be used to pay the firm's debts if P's own property is insufficient
P's private property is applied first to the firm's debts because firm's creditors have priority everywhere
questions.explanation:
Under Section 49, private property of a partner goes first to his private debts. Only the surplus may be used for the firm's debts.
(1) Wrong: the firm's property is applied first to the firm's debts.
(3) Wrong: a partner's private property does not include the personal property of his wife and children.
(4) Wrong: firm's creditors get priority only over the firm's property, not over the partner's private property.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution of a firm, the following information is given:
• Assets (other than cash) transferred to Realisation A/c at book value: Rs. 2,00,000. This includes debtors at gross value.
• Provision for doubtful debts: Rs. 2,000.
• Creditors: Rs. 50,000.
• Assets realised Rs. 1,80,000, and creditors were paid Rs. 48,000.
• An unrecorded asset was taken over by a partner for Rs. 5,000.
• Realisation expenses of Rs. 3,000 were paid by the firm.
What is the result of realisation?
options: Loss of Rs. 11,000
Loss of Rs. 14,000
Loss of Rs. 16,000
Loss of Rs. 19,000
questions.explanation:
Given: the figures listed in the question.
Debit side of Realisation A/c = assets 2,00,000 + creditors paid 48,000 + expenses 3,000 = Rs. 2,51,000.
Credit side of Realisation A/c = provision 2,000 + creditors 50,000 + bank (assets realised) 1,80,000 + partner's capital (unrecorded asset) 5,000 = Rs. 2,37,000.
Debit exceeds credit by 2,51,000 − 2,37,000 = Rs. 14,000.
So the result is a loss on realisation of Rs. 14,000.
The most tempting error is ignoring the provision, which gives Rs. 16,000.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution of a firm, the amount realised from assets is applied according to Section 48. How many of the following are paid BEFORE any amount is returned to partners on account of their capital?
(i) Sundry creditors
(ii) Bank overdraft
(iii) Loan advanced by a partner to the firm
(iv) Secured bank loan
(v) Residue to be divided in profit sharing ratio
(vi) Bills payable
questions.explanation:
Section 48(b) order: debts to third parties, then partners' loans (advances), then capital, then residue.
(i), (ii), (iv) and (vi) are outside debts, so they are paid first. Secured loans rank ahead of unsecured ones.
(iii) A partner's loan is paid after outside debts but before capital.
(v) The residue is distributed only after capital is repaid.
So five items are paid before capital.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution of a firm, how many of the following items will be transferred to the DEBIT side of the Realisation Account?
Stock; Sundry debtors (at gross value); Cash at bank; Goodwill appearing in the books; Debit balance of Profit and Loss Account; Plant and machinery
questions.explanation:
Debited to Realisation A/c at book value: stock, sundry debtors (gross value), goodwill (an intangible asset) and plant and machinery. That makes 4 items.
Not debited: cash at bank is used to make payments. The debit balance of Profit and Loss is a fictitious asset written off to the partners' capital accounts in their profit sharing ratio.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: A creditor’s ₹14,000 balance has been transferred to Realisation Account. In full settlement, the creditor accepts an unrecorded investment valued at ₹17,500 and pays the ₹3,500 excess to the firm. The firm also sells an unrecorded computer for ₹2,200 and pays an unrecorded repair bill of ₹1,200. If these are the only Realisation Account items, what is the profit on realisation?
questions.explanation:
Given: The creditor’s ₹14,000 balance is already credited to Realisation Account. The creditor’s extra ₹3,500 and computer proceeds of ₹2,200 are also credits.
No separate entry is made for the investment accepted in settlement. The ₹1,200 repair payment is a debit.
Substituting: Profit = ₹14,000 + ₹3,500 + ₹2,200 − ₹1,200 = ₹18,500.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: At the time of dissolution of a firm, which one of the following items appearing in the Balance Sheet is NOT transferred to the Realisation Account?
options: Sundry debtors
Bank overdraft
Partner's loan shown on the liabilities side
Bills receivable
questions.explanation:
Assets other than cash, bank and fictitious assets go to the debit of Realisation A/c, and external (third-party) liabilities go to its credit.
Sundry debtors and bills receivable are assets, so they are debited.
Bank overdraft is an external liability, so it is credited.
A partner's loan is an internal liability. It is paid off separately through the Bank A/c and never passes through the Realisation A/c.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Statement I: The death of a partner always results in the dissolution of the partnership firm.
Statement II: Dissolution of a firm on the happening of contingencies such as death or insolvency of a partner is subject to the contract between the partners.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Statement II is correct. Expiry of term, completion of venture, death and insolvency of a partner dissolve the firm 'subject to contract between the partners'.
Statement I is incorrect. Because of that condition, the partners may agree that the firm continues after a partner's death.
In that case, death dissolves only the partnership (a reconstitution), not the firm.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: A firm has 120 shares that were completely written off in its books. On dissolution, the partners take them over at ₹7 per share in their profit-sharing ratio of 3:2. How much is debited to the first partner’s capital account?
questions.explanation:
Given: 120 written-off shares are taken over at ₹7 each; the first partner’s share is 3 out of 5.
Formula: Debit to the first partner’s capital = total takeover value × 3/5.
Substituting: ₹(120 × 7) × 3/5 = ₹504.
So the first partner’s capital account is debited by ₹504. Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: A creditor is owed ₹18,000. During dissolution, the creditor accepts an unrecorded investment valued at ₹5,000 as part payment, and the firm pays the rest in cash. What amount is entered as a debit to Realisation Account for the cash payment?
questions.explanation:
Given: Creditor’s claim is ₹18,000; the unrecorded investment settles ₹5,000 of it.
The asset transferred to the creditor needs no separate entry. Only the cash payment is recorded.
Substituting: Cash paid = ₹18,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹13,000.
So Realisation Account is debited by ₹13,000 and Bank is credited. Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Event) with List-II (Mode of dissolution of a firm):
List-I
A. A partner becomes an alien enemy after war is declared between his country and India
B. The term for which the firm was constituted expires
C. A partner persistently commits breach of the partnership agreement
D. All partners consent to close the firm
List-II
(i) Dissolution by agreement
(ii) Compulsory dissolution
(iii) Dissolution on happening of contingencies
(iv) Dissolution by court
Choose the correct option:
options: A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(iv), D-(i)
A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(ii), D-(i)
A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(iii)
A-(iii), B-(ii), C-(i), D-(iv)
questions.explanation:
A: A partner becoming an alien enemy makes the partnership business unlawful, so it is compulsory dissolution → (ii).
B: Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency → (iii).
C: Persistent breach of the agreement is a ground the court considers on a partner's suit → (iv).
D: Consent of all partners is dissolution by agreement → (i).
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Kavya undertakes the dissolution work of her firm. Terms:
- She is to receive a remuneration of Rs 10,000.
- She agrees to bear dissolution expenses up to Rs 5,000.
- The actual dissolution expenses are Rs 7,000, all paid by Kavya herself.
What total amount will be debited to the Realisation Account and credited to Kavya's Capital Account?
questions.explanation:
Remuneration: Realisation A/c Dr. To Kavya's Capital A/c with Rs 10,000.
Expenses: Kavya bears only up to Rs 5,000. The excess, 7,000 - 5,000 = Rs 2,000, was paid by her on behalf of the firm. So Realisation A/c Dr. To Kavya's Capital A/c with Rs 2,000.
Total = 10,000 + 2,000 = Rs 12,000.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Case: Aman, Bela and Chirag formed a firm for a fixed term of 5 years. Their partnership deed states that the death of a partner shall not dissolve the firm. In the third year Chirag dies. Aman and Bela settle Chirag's dues with his legal heirs and continue the business under the same name. No partner approaches the court.
Which of the following correctly describes the legal position?
options: The firm is compulsorily dissolved on Chirag's death, because death of a partner always ends the firm
The firm is dissolved by court, because death makes a partner permanently incapable of performing his duties
The partnership among Aman, Bela and Chirag is dissolved, but the firm is not dissolved
The firm stands dissolved by notice, since the death of a partner converts it into a partnership at will
questions.explanation:
Death of a partner is a contingency. It dissolves the firm only subject to the contract between the partners. Here the deed provides that death will not dissolve the firm.
The old relationship among all three partners therefore ends, which is dissolution of partnership (reconstitution). The firm itself continues its business.
Option (1) fails because death is not a ground for compulsory dissolution.
Option (2) fails because no suit was filed in court.
Option (4) fails because the firm was formed for a fixed term, so it is not a partnership at will.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: X, Y and Z are partners. On the date of dissolution, the capitals of the solvent partners X and Y stand at ₹60,000 and ₹40,000 respectively. Z is declared insolvent, and the debit balance of ₹15,000 in his capital account cannot be recovered. There is no agreement among the partners on this point. Applying the Garner vs. Murray rule, how much of Z's deficiency will be borne by X?
questions.explanation:
Given: X ₹60,000, Y ₹40,000 (capitals on date of dissolution); Z's irrecoverable deficiency = ₹15,000.
Rule: under Garner vs. Murray, solvent partners bear the deficiency in their capital ratio, here 60,000 : 40,000 = 3 : 2.
X's share = 15,000 × 3/5 = ₹9,000. Y bears ₹6,000.
Option (1), ₹7,500, wrongly splits the loss equally.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Basis) with List-II (Position on dissolution of the FIRM):
List-I
(A) Termination of business
(B) Settlement of assets and liabilities
(C) Economic relationship between partners
(D) Books of account
List-II
(i) Assets are sold and liabilities are paid off
(ii) Are closed
(iii) Business of the firm is closed
(iv) Comes to an end
options: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(iii)
A-(iv), B-(i), C-(iii), D-(ii)
questions.explanation:
A-(iii): on dissolution of the firm, the business of the firm is closed.
B-(i): assets are sold and liabilities are paid off. They are not merely revalued.
C-(iv): the economic relationship between the partners comes to an end.
D-(ii): the books of account are closed.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: During the dissolution of a firm, realisation expenses of ₹9,000 were paid by Kavya, one of the partners, on behalf of the firm. There was no agreement that she would bear these expenses. Which journal entry will be recorded in the books of the firm?
options: Realisation A/c Dr. ₹9,000 To Kavya's Capital A/c ₹9,000
Kavya's Capital A/c Dr. ₹9,000 To Realisation A/c ₹9,000
Realisation A/c Dr. ₹9,000 To Bank A/c ₹9,000
Kavya's Capital A/c Dr. ₹9,000 To Bank A/c ₹9,000
questions.explanation:
The expenses belong to the firm because no partner has agreed to bear them, so Realisation A/c is debited.
Kavya paid them from her own pocket. The firm now owes her this amount, so her Capital A/c is credited.
Option (3) would be correct only if the firm had paid from its bank account.
Option (2) reverses the entry and would wrongly reduce Kavya's claim.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution of a firm, the following balances appear in its books:
Stock, Sundry Debtors (gross), Cash at Bank, Goodwill, Profit and Loss Account (debit balance), Machinery.
How many of these are transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account?
questions.explanation:
Rule: all assets are transferred to the debit of the Realisation Account at book value, except cash, bank and fictitious assets.
Transferred: Stock, Sundry Debtors (at gross value), Goodwill and Machinery. That makes 4.
Not transferred:
- Cash at Bank stays in the Bank Account.
- The debit balance of Profit and Loss is a fictitious asset. It is written off to partners' capital accounts in their profit sharing ratio.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, Mohan, a partner, takes over the firm's stock at an agreed value of Rs 24,000. The stock has already been transferred to the Realisation Account. Which journal entry records this?
options: Realisation A/c Dr. To Mohan's Capital A/c Rs 24,000
Mohan's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c Rs 24,000
Mohan's Capital A/c Dr. To Stock A/c Rs 24,000
Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c Rs 24,000
questions.explanation:
When a partner takes over an asset, the agreed value is a recovery for the firm, just like a sale. So the Realisation Account is credited.
The partner pays nothing in cash. The amount is charged to him, so his Capital Account is debited.
Option (3) is wrong because the Stock Account was already closed when stock was transferred to Realisation.
Option (4) applies only when an asset is sold for cash.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Under which section of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 is the dissolution of partnership between all the partners of a firm termed 'dissolution of the firm'?
options: Section 48
Section 49
Section 39
Section 42
questions.explanation:
Section 39 defines dissolution of a firm as the dissolution of partnership between all the partners of the firm.
Section 48 is a tempting option, but it lays down the rules for settling accounts after dissolution, such as the order of paying debts.
Section 49 deals with how firm's debts and partners' private debts are treated when both exist.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Case: Pranav, Qasim and Ritu are partners in a profitable trading firm. Their partnership deed fixes a term of 10 years, of which 4 years have passed. Without consulting the others, Qasim sells his entire interest in the firm to an outsider, Sahil. Pranav and Ritu do not wish to continue the business in this situation.
Which of the following is the correct legal position?
options: The firm stands compulsorily dissolved the moment Qasim transfers his interest
Pranav or Ritu may file a suit, and the court may order dissolution because a partner has transferred his whole interest to a third party
The firm cannot be dissolved before 10 years because its business is profitable
Pranav may dissolve the firm simply by giving written notice to the other partners
questions.explanation:
A partner transferring his whole interest to a third party is a ground for dissolution by court, on a partner's suit. So (b) is correct.
(a) is wrong because this event is not among the compulsory grounds (insolvency, illegality, unlawful event).
(c) is wrong because neither profitability nor an unexpired term stops a court from ordering dissolution.
(d) is wrong because dissolution by notice applies only to a partnership at will, and this is a fixed-term firm.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The court may order a partnership firm to be dissolved, at the suit of a partner, when another partner becomes insane.
Reason (R): A firm is compulsorily dissolved, without the intervention of the court, when any one partner becomes insane.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. Insanity of a partner is one of the grounds on which the court may order dissolution at the suit of a partner.
R is false. Compulsory dissolution applies only in these cases:
- all partners, or all but one partner, become insolvent;
- the business becomes illegal;
- an event makes it unlawful to carry on the business in partnership.
Insanity of a partner is not a case of compulsory dissolution.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following items are recorded on the CREDIT side of the Realisation Account at the time of dissolution?
(i) Stock taken over by a partner
(ii) Creditors paid in cash
(iii) Sale of an unrecorded asset
(iv) A partner agreeing to pay off a bank loan
(v) Cash received from a creditor who took over an asset worth more than his dues
(vi) Provision for doubtful debts
options: Two
Three
Four
Five
questions.explanation:
(i) Credit: Partner's Capital Dr. To Realisation.
(ii) Debit: Realisation Dr. To Bank.
(iii) Credit: Bank Dr. To Realisation.
(iv) Debit: Realisation Dr. To Partner's Capital.
(v) Credit: Bank Dr. To Realisation.
(vi) Credit: the provision is transferred along with the liabilities.
Credit-side items are (i), (iii), (v) and (vi), which makes four.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the statements regarding Section 49 of the Partnership Act, 1932.
Statement I: The firm's property is applied first to pay the firm's debts, and any surplus is divided among the partners as per their claims.
Statement II: The private property of a partner includes the personal property of his wife and children, which can be used to pay the firm's debts.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct: under Section 49(a), firm's property goes first to the firm's debts. The surplus is shared among partners as per their claims and can then be used for their private debts.
Statement II is incorrect: NCERT clearly states that a partner's private property does NOT include the personal property of his wife and children.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution, Manoj's capital account shows the following:
• Opening credit balance: Rs 50,000
• Share of General Reserve: Rs 6,000
• Assets taken over by him: Rs 80,000
• Share of loss on realisation: Rs 4,000
How much cash must Manoj bring in to settle his account, and which entry records it?
options: Rs 20,000; Bank A/c Dr. To Manoj's Capital A/c
Rs 28,000; Bank A/c Dr. To Manoj's Capital A/c
Rs 36,000; Manoj's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Rs 24,000; Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
questions.explanation:
Given: Credits = 50,000 + 6,000 = Rs 56,000. Debits = 80,000 + 4,000 = Rs 84,000.
Formula: Balance = Credits − Debits.
Substituting: 56,000 − 84,000 = −Rs 28,000. This is a debit balance.
A partner with a debit balance brings in cash. The entry is Bank A/c Dr. To Manoj's Capital A/c, with Rs 28,000.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On dissolution, sundry debtors are transferred to the Realisation Account at their gross (full book) value.
Reason (R): The provision for doubtful debts is separately transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: A is true. NCERT requires debtors to be transferred at gross value.
Step 2: R is true. The provision for doubtful debts is credited to the Realisation Account along with the liabilities.
Step 3: R explains A. Because the provision is carried to the credit side separately, the debtors must go to the debit side in full. Otherwise the provision would be counted twice.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: During dissolution, a firm sells an old typewriter for ₹900. It had been written off completely in an earlier year. Which entry records the sale?
options: Realisation A/c Dr. ₹900; To Bank A/c ₹900
Bank A/c Dr. ₹900; To Realisation A/c ₹900
Bank A/c Dr. ₹900; To Typewriter A/c ₹900
Typewriter A/c Dr. ₹900; To Realisation A/c ₹900
questions.explanation:
The typewriter has no balance in the books, so its account is not transferred to Realisation Account.
Cash received from selling an unrecorded asset is debited to Bank and credited to Realisation Account.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: At the time of dissolution of a firm, which one of the following balances is NOT transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account?
options: Goodwill
Stock
Cash at bank
Investments
questions.explanation:
Step 1: All assets are transferred to the debit of Realisation Account at book value. Cash in hand, bank balance and fictitious assets are the exceptions.
Step 2: Goodwill, stock and investments are all assets, so they are transferred.
Step 3: Cash at bank is not transferred. It is the account through which assets are realised and liabilities are paid, and it is closed last when partners are settled.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Under Section 48 of the Partnership Act, 1932, losses arising on dissolution, including deficiencies of capital, are paid in a set order unless the partners have agreed otherwise. From which source are such losses met FIRST?
options: Out of the capital of the partners
By the partners individually in their profit sharing ratio
Out of profits
By the partners individually in their capital ratio
questions.explanation:
Section 48(a) fixes the order for meeting losses: first out of profits, next out of partners' capital, and lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in their profit sharing ratio.
Option (1) is the second source, not the first.
Option (2) is the last resort, not the first.
Option (4) uses the wrong ratio. Personal contribution is in the profit sharing ratio, not the capital ratio.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On which of the following grounds may a court, at the suit of a partner, order the dissolution of a firm?
options: All the partners have become insolvent
The venture for which the firm was formed has been completed
All the partners have agreed to dissolve the firm
A partner has transferred the whole of his interest in the firm to a third party
questions.explanation:
The court may order dissolution when a partner transfers his whole interest in the firm to a third party. This is one of the seven grounds listed for dissolution by court.
Insolvency of all partners causes compulsory dissolution, so no court order is needed.
Completion of the venture is a contingency.
Consent of all partners is dissolution by agreement.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (item on dissolution) with List-II (accounting treatment):
List-I
(A) Partner's loan shown on the liabilities side
(B) General Reserve
(C) Unrecorded asset taken over by a partner
(D) Credit balance in a partner's current account
List-II
(i) Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
(ii) Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iii) Distributed among all partners' capital accounts in the profit sharing ratio
(iv) Transferred to that partner's own capital account
options: A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(iv)
A-(i), B-(iii), C-(ii), D-(iv)
A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(iv), D-(i)
A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(ii)
questions.explanation:
(A)-(ii): A partner's loan is not taken to the Realisation Account. It is paid directly through the bank.
(B)-(iii): Accumulated profits such as reserves are credited to the partners' capital accounts in the profit sharing ratio.
(C)-(i): An asset taken over by a partner is debited to his capital account and credited to the Realisation Account.
(D)-(iv): A current account balance is closed by transfer to the same partner's capital account, as in Illustration 4.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, a creditor to whom Rs 25,000 is due accepts furniture (already transferred to Realisation Account) in full and final settlement of his claim. The journal entry required is:
options: Realisation A/c Dr. To Furniture A/c Rs 25,000
Creditors A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c Rs 25,000
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c Rs 25,000
No journal entry is required
questions.explanation:
When a creditor accepts an asset in full and final settlement, no cash moves.
Both the asset and the creditor are already in the Realisation Account, on the debit and credit sides respectively. So no entry is needed.
Option (2) is the transfer entry. It is passed earlier when all liabilities are moved to the Realisation Account, not for this settlement.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution, the Balance Sheet of a firm shows the following assets:
Sundry debtors Rs. 50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts Rs. 2,000; Stock Rs. 30,000; Machinery Rs. 70,000; Goodwill Rs. 10,000; Cash in hand Rs. 8,000; Bank balance Rs. 12,000; Profit and Loss A/c (debit balance) Rs. 5,000.
What amount will be debited to the Realisation Account for the transfer of assets?
questions.explanation:
Rule: transfer all assets at book value, except cash, bank and fictitious assets. Debtors are transferred at their gross value.
Assets transferred: Debtors 50,000 + Stock 30,000 + Machinery 70,000 + Goodwill 10,000 = Rs. 1,60,000.
The provision of Rs. 2,000 is credited separately, so net debtors are not used.
The Profit and Loss debit balance is a fictitious asset and goes to the capital accounts.
Cash and bank are excluded.
So the amount debited = Rs. 1,60,000.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of the firm of Amit and Sumit, Mrs. Amit's loan of Rs 40,000 has already been transferred to the Realisation Account. Amit agrees to take over his wife's loan. Which journal entry records this?
options: Mrs. Amit's Loan A/c Dr. To Amit's Capital A/c
Amit's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
Realisation A/c Dr. To Amit's Capital A/c
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
questions.explanation:
Mrs. Amit is an outside party, so her loan is an external liability. It is credited to the Realisation Account and the loan account is closed.
When a partner takes responsibility for a liability, the liability is settled on the firm's behalf. So Realisation A/c is debited and the partner's capital is credited, because the firm owes him that amount.
Option (1) is wrong because the loan account has already been closed. Option (4) would apply only if the firm paid in cash.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Xavier and Yamini, equal partners, dissolve their firm. The bank balance was ₹6,000, and assets were realised for ₹90,000. Creditors were paid ₹40,000 and realisation expenses of ₹2,000. Xavier's loan of ₹10,000 to the firm was repaid. A loan of ₹5,000 earlier given by the firm to Yamini was recovered in cash. After all adjustments, Yamini's capital account showed a debit balance of ₹4,000, which she paid in cash. What amount is finally paid to Xavier to close his capital account?
questions.explanation:
Rule: after Yamini clears her debit balance, Xavier is the only partner with a credit balance. So he receives exactly the cash remaining in the bank.
Cash in: 6,000 + 90,000 + 5,000 (loan recovered) + 4,000 (Yamini's cash) = 1,05,000.
Cash out before Xavier: 40,000 + 2,000 + 10,000 (Xavier's loan) = 52,000.
Payment to Xavier = 1,05,000 − 52,000 = ₹53,000.
Option (2) wrongly ignores both receipts from Yamini.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When a partner agrees to discharge a liability of the firm on its dissolution, Realisation Account is debited and that partner's Capital Account is credited.
Reason (R): By paying the firm's liability, the partner has settled an obligation of the firm, so the firm now owes that amount to the partner.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. The liability was transferred to the credit of the Realisation Account. Its settlement is therefore debited to the Realisation Account, and because the partner pays it, his Capital Account is credited.
R is true. The partner's payment increases his claim on the firm.
R explains why his Capital Account, and not Bank, is credited.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When a partner has agreed to bear the realisation expenses and he himself pays them, no journal entry is recorded in the books of the firm.
Reason (R): In this case the expenses are the partner's own burden, and neither the firm's cash nor the firm's Realisation Account is affected.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is true. NCERT states that if the partner who agreed to bear the expenses pays them himself, no entry is required.
R is true. The burden is entirely the partner's own. No firm cash goes out, and nothing is chargeable to the Realisation Account.
R therefore explains why no entry arises.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, the amount realised from assets is used first to pay the firm's debts to third parties. Under Section 48 of the Partnership Act, 1932, what is paid out of the remaining amount next?
options: Each partner's capital, proportionately
Each partner's loans and advances to the firm, proportionately
The private debts of the partners
The residue, divided among partners in their profit sharing ratio
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Case: A and B share profits in the ratio 3:2 and dissolve their firm. Capitals are A Rs. 50,000 and B Rs. 30,000. General Reserve is Rs. 10,000. B's loan to the firm of Rs. 8,000 is paid separately. On realisation, A takes over stock at Rs. 12,000, and the Realisation Account finally shows a loss of Rs. 15,000. What amount will finally be paid to A to settle his capital account?
questions.explanation:
Given: profit sharing ratio 3:2.
Credit A's capital: opening balance 50,000 + reserve share (3/5 × 10,000) 6,000 = 56,000.
Debit A's capital: realisation loss share (3/5 × 15,000) 9,000 + stock taken over 12,000 = 21,000.
So, the amount paid to A = 56,000 − 21,000 = Rs. 35,000. B's loan does not affect A's account. Forgetting the stock taken over gives Rs. 47,000.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways in which a partnership (not the firm) gets dissolved, as listed in NCERT?
options: Admission of a new partner
Change in the existing profit-sharing ratio among partners
The business of the firm becoming illegal
Retirement of a partner
questions.explanation:
NCERT lists seven ways a partnership is dissolved: change in profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement, death, insolvency of a partner, completion of the venture and expiry of the term.
When the business of a firm becomes illegal, the firm itself is compulsorily dissolved. It is not a case of reconstitution.
Admission, change in ratio and retirement all appear in the list.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Mode of dissolution of a firm) with List-II (Situation):
List-I
(a) Compulsory dissolution
(b) Dissolution by notice
(c) Dissolution by court
(d) Dissolution on happening of contingencies
List-II
(i) A partner of a partnership at will gives written notice of his intention to dissolve
(ii) The business of the firm becomes illegal
(iii) The fixed term for which the firm was constituted expires
(iv) A partner persistently commits breach of the partnership agreement
questions.explanation:
(a)-(ii): Illegality of the business causes compulsory dissolution.
(b)-(i): In a partnership at will, any one partner may dissolve the firm by giving written notice.
(c)-(iv): Persistent breach of the agreement is a ground on which the court may order dissolution.
(d)-(iii): Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency that dissolves the firm, subject to contract.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a partner's loan appearing on the liabilities side of the balance sheet at the time of dissolution is correct?
options: It is transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account.
It is transferred to the partner's capital account.
It is not transferred to the Realisation Account; it is paid directly through Cash/Bank after outside liabilities.
It is transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Only external liabilities are transferred to the Realisation Account. A partner's loan is not an external liability.
Step 2: Under Section 48, partners' loans are repaid after third-party debts and before capital. The entry is Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
Step 3: Option (2) is tempting, but the loan has priority over capital, so it is not merged with capital.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Statement I: The Revaluation Account records only the increase or decrease in the values of assets and liabilities, whereas the Realisation Account records the full book values of the assets and external liabilities transferred to it.
Statement II: Like the Realisation Account, the Revaluation Account requires the books of account of the firm to be closed.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct. On reconstitution, only the changes in value pass through the Revaluation A/c. On dissolution, assets and external liabilities are transferred at their full book values to the Realisation A/c.
Statement II is incorrect. Revaluation happens on reconstitution, when the business continues and a new balance sheet is drawn. Only dissolution of the firm requires the books to be closed.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which one of the following is a ground on which a firm is dissolved only by the order of a court, at the suit of a partner?
options: The business of the firm becomes illegal
All the partners, or all but one partner, become insolvent
A partner becomes insane
The fixed term for which the firm was constituted expires
questions.explanation:
Insanity of a partner is a ground for dissolution by court. The court acts on the suit of a partner.
Illegality of the business causes compulsory dissolution. No court order is needed.
Insolvency of all partners, or of all but one, also causes compulsory dissolution.
Expiry of a fixed term dissolves the firm on the happening of a contingency, subject to the partnership contract.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
On dissolution of a firm, how many of the following are paid out of the realised assets BEFORE the partners' capital balances are settled?
(i) Bank overdraft
(ii) Loan given to the firm by a partner
(iii) Bills payable
(iv) Loan from a bank secured on stock
(v) Surplus remaining after all claims
questions.explanation:
(i) Bank overdraft: an outside liability, so it is paid before capital.
(ii) Partner's loan: an advance distinguished from capital, so it is paid before capital.
(iii) Bills payable: an outside liability, paid before capital.
(iv) Secured bank loan: an outside liability, and secured loans are paid first of all.
(v) Surplus: the residue is shared in profit-sharing ratio only AFTER capitals are settled.
So four items are paid before capital.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A firm of three partners is compulsorily dissolved when any one of the partners is declared insolvent.
Reason (R): An insolvent person becomes incompetent to enter into a contract.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
A is false. Compulsory dissolution applies only when all the partners, or all but one partner, become insolvent. The insolvency of a single partner out of three is a contingency. It dissolves the firm only subject to the contract between the partners.
R is true. Insolvency makes a person incompetent to sign a contract. This is why compulsory dissolution follows when all, or all but one, partners are insolvent.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (transaction on dissolution) with List-II (journal treatment):
List-I
A. Furniture sold for cash
B. Investments taken over by partner X
C. Partner Y agrees to pay the bills payable
D. Creditor accepts machinery in full settlement
List-II
(i) X's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
(ii) No entry
(iii) Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
(iv) Realisation A/c Dr. To Y's Capital A/c
options: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(i), B-(iii), C-(ii), D-(iv)
A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(iii)
questions.explanation:
A: A cash sale of an asset brings money into the firm, so Bank Dr. To Realisation, which is (iii).
B: The partner taking over an asset is charged with it, so his capital is debited, which is (i).
C: A partner paying a firm's liability is credited, and Realisation is debited, which is (iv).
D: An asset accepted by a creditor in full settlement needs no entry, which is (ii).
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
How many of the following are grounds on which a court may order dissolution of a firm at the suit of a partner?
(i) A partner becomes insane
(ii) A partner becomes permanently incapable of performing his duties
(iii) The business can be carried on only at a loss
(iv) The business of the firm becomes illegal
(v) A partner dies
(vi) A partner is guilty of misconduct likely to adversely affect the business
options: Three
Four
Five
Six
questions.explanation:
(i) Court ground: insanity of a partner.
(ii) Court ground: permanent incapacity.
(iii) Court ground: the business can be carried on only at a loss.
(iv) Not a court ground. Illegality of business causes compulsory dissolution.
(v) Not a court ground. Death of a partner is a contingency, subject to contract.
(vi) Court ground: misconduct adversely affecting the business.
So the count is 4.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: A creditor to whom Rs. 30,000 is due accepts machinery valued at Rs. 24,000 and the balance in cash, in full settlement of his claim. What amount will be credited to the Bank Account for this settlement?
questions.explanation:
Given: Dues = Rs. 30,000; machinery accepted = Rs. 24,000.
Rule: When a creditor accepts an asset as part payment, an entry is passed only for the cash paid.
Cash paid = 30,000 − 24,000 = Rs. 6,000.
Entry: Realisation A/c Dr. 6,000, To Bank A/c 6,000.
So Bank is credited with Rs. 6,000. The machinery handed over needs no entry.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Match List-I (situation on dissolution) with List-II (journal entry):
List-I
A. Realisation expenses paid by a partner on behalf of the firm
B. A partner agreed to bear the realisation expenses, but the firm pays them
C. A creditor accepts an asset in full and final settlement of his dues
D. An unrecorded asset is sold for cash
List-II
(i) No entry
(ii) Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
(iii) Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
(iv) Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
options: A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)
A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(ii), D-(i)
A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(i), D-(iv)
questions.explanation:
A-(iv): The expense belongs to the firm, so Realisation A/c is debited. The partner who paid it is credited.
B-(iii): The expense is the partner's own burden, so his capital is debited. Bank is credited.
C-(i): The asset and the creditor are both already in Realisation A/c, so no entry is passed.
D-(ii): Cash received for an unrecorded asset is credited to Realisation A/c.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
During dissolution of the firm of Arti and Karim, the following transactions took place:
(i) An outstanding bill for repairs, not recorded in the books, was paid.
(ii) Rs. 1,200 was recovered from a debtor written off as bad last year.
(iii) A bill discounted with the bank was dishonoured and the firm paid the amount (contingent liability materialised).
(iv) Compensation of Rs. 40,000 was paid to employees.
(v) Unrecorded goodwill was taken over by Arti.
How many of these transactions are recorded by debiting the Realisation Account?
questions.explanation:
(i) Debit: payment of an unrecorded liability is Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
(ii) Credit: bad debts recovered are Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c.
(iii) Debit: a contingent liability that is paid is treated like an unrecorded liability, so Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
(iv) Debit: compensation paid to employees is Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
(v) Credit: goodwill taken over by a partner is Arti's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c.
Three items, (i), (iii) and (iv), are debited.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution, creditors of Rs 50,000 accept machinery (book value Rs 55,000, already transferred to the Realisation Account) in full and final settlement of their claim. What entry is passed for this settlement?
options: Creditors A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c Rs 50,000
Realisation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c Rs 55,000
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c Rs 50,000
No entry is required
questions.explanation:
The creditors (Rs 50,000) are already on the credit side of the Realisation Account.
The machinery (Rs 55,000) is already on the debit side.
Both accounts are therefore closed, and no cash changes hands. Any difference automatically becomes part of the realisation profit or loss.
So, as per NCERT, no journal entry is needed.
Option (3) would wrongly record a cash payment that never happened.
Answer: (4)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Read the two statements about closing the books of a dissolved firm.
Statement I: General Reserve appearing in the Balance Sheet is transferred to the partners' capital accounts in their profit sharing ratio.
Statement II: A partner's current account showing a debit balance is transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct. Accumulated profits such as General Reserve are credited to the partners' capital accounts in their profit sharing ratio. The entry is General Reserve A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs.
Statement II is incorrect. A current account is never taken to the Realisation Account. Its balance is transferred to the same partner's Capital Account, as in the Nayana–Arushi illustration.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Arjun and Bina share profits in the ratio 3:2. On dissolution, Arjun's capital account showed a credit balance of ₹80,000 and the General Reserve was ₹30,000. Arjun took over furniture at ₹12,000, and the loss on realisation was ₹15,000. What amount will Arjun finally receive from the firm?
questions.explanation:
Given: Arjun's capital ₹80,000 (Cr.); General Reserve ₹30,000; loss ₹15,000; ratio 3:2; furniture taken over ₹12,000.
Credits to Arjun: capital 80,000 + reserve share (3/5 × 30,000) 18,000 = 98,000.
Debits to Arjun: loss share (3/5 × 15,000) 9,000 + furniture 12,000 = 21,000.
Final amount = 98,000 − 21,000 = ₹77,000.
The furniture is debited to Arjun because he takes over an asset instead of receiving cash.
Answer: (1)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, Neha, a partner, takes over the firm's stock at an agreed value of Rs. 18,000. Stock has already been transferred to the Realisation Account. Which journal entry records this transaction?
options:
Realisation A/c Dr. 18,000
To Neha's Capital A/c 18,000

Neha's Capital A/c Dr. 18,000
To Realisation A/c 18,000

Bank A/c Dr. 18,000
To Realisation A/c 18,000

Neha's Capital A/c Dr. 18,000
To Stock A/c 18,000
questions.explanation:
When a partner takes over an asset, the firm receives no cash. Instead, the partner's claim on the firm falls by the agreed value.
So the partner's capital account is debited, and the Realisation Account is credited, just as it would be for a sale.
Option (1) is the entry for a liability that a partner assumes, so it is the reverse of what is needed.
Option (3) would apply only if cash were actually received.
Option (4) is wrong because stock has already been closed to the Realisation Account.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On the dissolution of a partnership (for example, on the admission of a new partner), how are the assets and liabilities of the firm dealt with?
options: They are sold and paid off, and the surplus is distributed among partners
They are revalued and a new balance sheet is drawn up
They are transferred to the Realisation Account at book value
They are distributed among the partners in their capital ratio
questions.explanation:
On dissolution of partnership, the firm's business continues and only the relationship among partners changes.
So assets and liabilities are revalued and a new balance sheet is prepared.
Selling assets and paying off liabilities through a Realisation Account happens only on dissolution of the firm, so option (1) and option (3) describe the wrong case.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: A firm’s goodwill is not recorded in its books. On dissolution, partner Kavya takes it over at an agreed value. Which accounts are affected?
options: Debit Goodwill Account; credit Kavya’s Capital Account
Debit Realisation Account; credit Kavya’s Capital Account
Debit Kavya’s Capital Account; credit Realisation Account
Debit Bank Account; credit Realisation Account
questions.explanation:
Goodwill is unrecorded, so there is no book balance to transfer.
Kavya receives an asset instead of cash, so her Capital Account is debited and Realisation Account is credited. Bank is unaffected.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Which of the following journal entries for realisation expenses on dissolution is INCORRECT?
options: Expenses paid by the firm: Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Expenses paid by a partner on behalf of the firm: Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
A partner has agreed to bear the expenses and pays them himself: Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
A partner has agreed to bear the expenses but the firm pays them: Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
questions.explanation:
(1) Correct: the firm bears the expense and pays it from the bank.
(2) Correct: the firm's expense is paid by a partner, so the firm owes him and his capital account is credited.
(3) Incorrect: if the partner who has agreed to bear the expenses pays them himself, it is his own burden. No entry is required.
(4) Correct: the firm pays on behalf of the partner, so his capital account is debited.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
X and Y share profits in the ratio 3:2. Their Balance Sheet on the date of dissolution was:
Liabilities: Creditors Rs 40,000; Y's Loan Rs 10,000; General Reserve Rs 15,000; Capitals – X Rs 60,000, Y Rs 40,000.
Assets: Bank Rs 10,000; Stock Rs 30,000; Debtors Rs 45,000; Machinery Rs 80,000.
The dissolution was completed as follows:
• X took over the stock at Rs 27,000.
• Debtors realised Rs 42,000 and machinery was sold for Rs 86,000.
• Creditors were paid Rs 39,000 in full settlement.
• Realisation expenses of Rs 3,000 were paid by the firm.
What amount is finally paid to Y on account of his capital?
questions.explanation:
Realisation A/c Dr. side: assets 1,55,000 + creditors 39,000 + expenses 3,000 = Rs 1,97,000.
Realisation A/c Cr. side: creditors 40,000 + X (stock) 27,000 + bank 1,28,000 = Rs 1,95,000.
Loss on realisation = Rs 2,000. Y's share = 2,000 × 2/5 = Rs 800.
Y's capital = 40,000 + reserve share 6,000 − 800 = Rs 45,200.
Y's loan of Rs 10,000 is paid separately, before capitals, so Rs 55,200 is wrong.
Check: Bank 10,000 + 1,28,000 − 39,000 − 3,000 − 10,000 = Rs 86,000. This equals X's Rs 40,800 + Y's Rs 45,200.
Answer: (2)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, creditors of Rs 50,000 accepted machinery valued at Rs 35,000 and the balance in cash in full settlement. What amount will be recorded in the entry 'Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c'?
questions.explanation:
Given: Creditors = Rs 50,000. Machinery accepted = Rs 35,000. Balance paid in cash.
Rule: when a creditor accepts an asset as part payment, an entry is made only for the cash paid.
Cash paid = 50,000 − 35,000 = Rs 15,000.
So Realisation A/c is debited and Bank A/c is credited with Rs 15,000.
Answer: (3)
questions.basis: NCERT Class 12 Accountancy · Dissolution of Partnership Firm

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question: Rahul, a partner, has private assets and private debts, and the firm's liabilities exceed its assets. As per Section 49 of the Partnership Act, 1932, Rahul's private property will be applied:
options: first towards the firm's debts and then towards his private debts
first towards his private debts, and the surplus, if any, towards the firm's debts
towards firm's debts and private debts in the ratio of their amounts
only towards his private debts, never towards the firm's debts
questions.explanation:
Under Section 49, a partner's private property is used first to pay his private debts.
Only the surplus, which is his net private assets, may be used for the firm's debts when the firm's liabilities exceed its assets.
Option (1) reverses this order. That order applies to the firm's property, which goes first to the firm's debts.
Answer: (2)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When Ravi, a partner, agrees to pay off his wife's loan of ₹30,000 to the firm, the entry passed is Realisation A/c Dr. To Ravi's Capital A/c ₹30,000.
Reason (R): By paying the loan, Ravi discharges a liability of the firm on its behalf, so this amount becomes due to him from the firm.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation:
A is true. Mrs. Ravi's loan is an outside liability, so it was first credited to the Realisation Account. When Ravi takes up its payment, Realisation A/c is debited and Ravi's Capital A/c is credited.
R is true. Ravi pays the firm's liability out of his own pocket, so the firm owes him that amount. This is exactly why his capital account is credited.
Therefore R correctly explains A.
Answer: (1)

Case: Rohan, Simran and Kabir are dissolving their firm. Rohan is appointed to complete the dissolution for a remuneration of ₹12,000. He agrees to bear all realisation expenses. Actual expenses of ₹9,000 are paid by the firm.
By how much will these arrangements reduce the profit (or increase the loss) shown by Realisation Account?
questions.explanation:
Remuneration: Realisation A/c Dr. To Rohan's Capital A/c ₹12,000. This is charged to Realisation Account.
Expenses are Rohan's burden, though the firm paid them: Rohan's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c ₹9,000. This is not charged to Realisation Account.
Only ₹12,000 is debited to Realisation Account.
The net credit of ₹3,000 to Rohan's capital is a distractor: it is not the effect on realisation.
Answer: (1)
